README.md.overview: The project README and the starting point of the guided tour (Step 1). It introduces BITS reports as a full-stack campus IT reporting app for CS F213, explains manual, scripted and Docker setup, lists seeded demo accounts, and documents Google sign-in, AI configuration, logging, two-step sign-in, SLA targets and non-IT emergency detection. Its feature table and OOP design map tell you which backend file implements each requirement, so it doubles as an index for the later tour steps.

sections.title: Title and technology stack
sections.explanation: States the app's purpose and lists the stack: a React frontend, a FastAPI + Pydantic + Motor backend, MongoDB, and JWT + bcrypt authentication. The last bullets name the design ideas (Strategy and State patterns, service-layer composition, custom exceptions) and the 'intelligent' features, which the tour covers in Steps 6-11.

sections.title: Manual local setup
sections.explanation: The three-part manual setup: run MongoDB on localhost:27017 (or point `backend/.env` elsewhere), create a virtualenv and start the API with `uvicorn server:app --reload --port 8000`, then `npm start` the frontend on port 3000. The `server:app` target refers to the `app` object in `backend/server.py`, the entry point explained in Step 2.

sections.title: One-command quick start
sections.explanation: Describes the `start.sh` / `start.bat` scripts that create settings files, the Python environment and packages, start MongoDB and launch both servers, plus optional ngrok and Docker Compose routes. Note the closing line: Gemini and SMTP keys are optional, and the app falls back to built-in behaviour without them. The scripts themselves are covered in the final tour step.

sections.title: Seeded demo accounts
sections.explanation: Lists the admin, customer and technician credentials created at startup by `app/services/seed.py`. The warning to change the admin password and JWT secret matters because both defaults are public in this file.

sections.title: Google sign-in and AI settings
sections.explanation: Documents the `.env` variables for Google OAuth, the allowed Workspace email domain, secure cookies and the optional Gemini model. It also explains why phones need an HTTPS tunnel for Google sign-in, and states the security rule implemented in `routers/auth.py`: the backend verifies every ID token and Google sign-in never elevates an existing user's role.

sections.title: Error logs and request ids
sections.explanation: Explains the human-readable logging produced by `logging_config.py` and `error_handling.py`: `app.log` versus `errors.log`, the indented 'What happened / Where / Likely cause' block, and the `X-Request-ID` that ties a user's error message to a log line. It also lists the tuning knobs (`LOG_LEVEL`, `LOG_DIR`, `SLOW_REQUEST_MS`, `LOG_FULL_TRACEBACKS`).

sections.title: AI safety and Mermaid notes
sections.explanation: Two short design notes. AI credentials stay on the server and the AI endpoint only suggests editable fields, never creating a report itself. Mermaid diagrams are deliberately absent because of a Node version constraint.

sections.title: Feature-to-code map
sections.explanation: A table mapping each project-brief requirement to the class or file that implements it, such as `WeightedScorePriorityStrategy`, `SlaMonitor`, `NotificationChannel` subclasses and `AuditObserver`. Use it as a lookup table while following the tour.

sections.title: Account security and two-step sign-in
sections.explanation: Covers the account page, TOTP two-step sign-in (a 5-minute sign-in pass, then a code; secrets encrypted at rest, backup codes stored as HMAC hashes), and session versioning that signs out other devices. It then documents the default SLA targets with their 25% at-risk window, the concept-based duplicate detector, and the offline scope rules that turn non-IT emergencies into help-line popups instead of tickets.

sections.title: OOP design and tests
sections.explanation: Gives the folder layout of the backend and explains where each OOP principle and design pattern (Strategy, State, Factory, Observer, Repository, Adapter, Template Method, composition root) appears. It ends with the custom exception list and the pytest instructions; tests need MongoDB and use a separate `itsm_test` database.

backend/requirements.txt.overview: The pinned Python dependency list for the FastAPI backend, referenced in Step 1 of the tour as an at-a-glance view of the backend's building blocks. Every package is pinned to an exact version so that local, scripted and Docker installs behave the same.

sections.title: Web framework and database
sections.explanation: FastAPI and Uvicorn (with the `standard` extras for faster event loop and reload support) serve the API, and Pydantic validates request bodies. Motor is the asyncio MongoDB driver used in `app/core/db.py`, built on the pinned PyMongo version. python-dotenv loads `backend/.env` at the top of `server.py`.

sections.title: Authentication primitives
sections.explanation: PyJWT signs and verifies the HS256 access, refresh and MFA tokens, and bcrypt hashes passwords and reset codes. Both are used directly in `app/core/security.py`.

sections.title: Testing tools
sections.explanation: pytest runs the test suite. httpx is listed here because the tests drive the FastAPI app through an httpx ASGI client; the logging code also recognises httpx timeouts when explaining external-service failures.

sections.title: Google sign-in, 2FA and crypto
sections.explanation: google-auth and requests verify Google ID tokens server-side in `routers/auth.py`. pyotp generates and checks TOTP codes for two-step sign-in, qrcode renders the setup QR code, and cryptography provides the Fernet encryption the README says protects stored TOTP secrets.

backend/app/core/db.py.overview: Creates the single shared Motor client and database handle used by every repository, and contains the startup routine that pings MongoDB, creates indexes and seeds data. `init_db` is awaited from the lifespan hook in `server.py`, making this file the database half of the startup sequence in Tour Step 2.

sections.title: Module-level client and database
sections.explanation: The `AsyncIOMotorClient` and `db` handle are created at import time from `MONGO_URL` and `DB_NAME`. Because these environment variables are read on import, `server.py` must call `load_dotenv` before importing this module. Motor connects lazily, so creating the client does not fail even if MongoDB is down; the first real command does.

sections.title: Index creation
sections.explanation: `ensure_indexes` declares the unique keys (user email, incident number) and the compound indexes that back common queries such as status/priority filters and newest-first audit and notification lists. The `expireAfterSeconds=0` indexes on `expires_at` make MongoDB delete password-reset records at the stored expiry time, and `security_events` expire after 90 days. Unique names for categories and services are attempted inside a try/except so that an older database with duplicate names logs a warning instead of blocking startup.

sections.title: Startup with retries and seeding
sections.explanation: `init_db` pings the server, builds indexes and runs `seed_all`, retrying up to 15 times with a 2-second delay; this lets the API start before MongoDB is ready, which is common under Docker Compose. Intermediate failures are logged as warnings without tracebacks, and only the final failure logs an error with a traceback and re-raises. The seed and logging imports are inside the function, which avoids an import cycle (`seed.py` imports `security.py`, which imports this module).

backend/app/core/error_handling.py.overview: Request logging middleware and the global exception handlers for the API. Every request gets a short request id, one access-log line, and, on failure, a clean JSON body plus a detailed log entry explaining what happened, who triggered it, where in the code it broke and the likely cause. It is registered by `server.py` and is part of the startup and cross-cutting infrastructure described in Tour Step 2; it is also where the domain's `ITSMError` hierarchy becomes HTTP responses.

sections.title: Purpose, imports and slow threshold
sections.explanation: The module docstring summarises the four guarantees: request ids, one access line per request, explained error logs, and JSON 500s that still carry CORS headers. Two named loggers (`http` and `errors`) separate access lines from error entries. `SLOW_REQUEST_MS` (default 1500) controls when a successful request is logged as a warning.

sections.title: Hint tables
sections.explanation: `STATUS_HINTS` maps HTTP status codes and `ITSM_HINTS` maps domain exception class names to a plain-English 'Likely cause'. The ITSM hints are more specific and are tried first in `itsm_error_handler`, falling back to the status-code hint. Keeping these as data makes it easy to add guidance for a new exception without touching handler code.

sections.title: Helpers and identifying the user
sections.explanation: `_is_database_outage` detects PyMongo connection failures so they can become a 503. `identify_user` decodes the JWT from the Authorization header or the `access_token` cookie without a database call, so even failing requests can be attributed to a user in the logs, and it distinguishes expired from invalid tokens. `_request_details` and `_rid` read the per-request context set by the middleware, falling back to a fresh id outside a request.

sections.title: Request logging middleware
sections.explanation: `RequestLoggingMiddleware` reuses an incoming `X-Request-ID` only if it matches a strict alphanumeric pattern, which prevents log injection; otherwise it generates an 8-character id. It stores the id, user and client in the `request_ctx` context variable so every log line written during the request is tagged. Any exception that no handler dealt with is logged with timing and turned into a JSON 500, or a 503 for database outages. Health checks are logged at DEBUG, slow requests as warnings, and the context is always reset in `finally`.

sections.title: Domain error handler
sections.explanation: Handles any `ITSMError` raised by the domain or services, using the exception's own `status_code` and `message`. These are expected business-rule refusals, so they are logged as warnings with the code location from `where_in_code`. The response includes the error class name, the request id and any `extra` fields the exception carries, such as duplicate-incident details.

sections.title: HTTP exception handler
sections.explanation: Handles `HTTPException`s raised by routes and by Starlette itself, including unmatched routes. A bare 404 'Not Found' gets a special hint about the `/api` prefix and HTTP method. 5xx codes are logged as errors and everything else as warnings, and any headers on the exception (for example `WWW-Authenticate`) are passed through to the response.

sections.title: Validation error handler
sections.explanation: Turns Pydantic `RequestValidationError`s into a readable bullet list of field problems for the log. Values of sensitive fields such as passwords, codes or tokens are replaced with `[hidden]` both in the log and in the JSON response, using `is_sensitive` from `logging_config.py`. The hint points developers to `app/models/schemas.py`, where the field rules live.

sections.title: Registering everything
sections.explanation: `register_error_handling` installs the middleware and the three exception handlers on the app. Its docstring states the ordering requirement that `server.py` follows: register this before adding `CORSMiddleware`, so that CORS wraps the error responses and the browser can read their message.

backend/app/core/logging_config.py.overview: Configures human-readable logging for the backend: a console handler plus rotating `app.log` and `errors.log` files, a formatter that prints a summary line followed by an indented details block, and helpers that redact secrets, locate the failing project line and translate common exceptions into plain-English causes and fixes. `server.py` calls `setup_logging()` before any other app import, and `error_handling.py` and `db.py` use `log_exception`, which is why this file belongs to the startup infrastructure in Tour Step 2.

sections.title: Format description and request context
sections.explanation: The docstring shows the exact log line format and the two output files. `BACKEND_ROOT` is computed from this file's location so project paths can be shown relative to `backend/`. `request_ctx` is a `ContextVar`, which keeps request data separate between concurrent asyncio requests where a plain global would mix them up.

sections.title: Redaction helpers
sections.explanation: `is_sensitive` flags field names that contain words like password, token or secret, plus an exact-match list for short names such as `code` and `key`. `redact` recursively hides those values, caps lists at 20 items and strings at 300 characters, and has a depth limit to stop runaway recursion. `redact_url` hides credentials in connection strings like `MONGO_URL`, and `short` truncates a value's repr for log messages.

sections.title: Context filter and project paths
sections.explanation: `_ContextFilter` copies the current request id onto each log record so the formatter can print it. `_project_path` returns a path relative to `backend/` only for the project's own files, returning `None` for virtualenv or site-packages files. `_PLUMBING` excludes `error_handling.py` so that log locations point at the code that actually failed, not the handler.

sections.title: Project-focused tracebacks
sections.explanation: `format_traceback` builds a shortened traceback that hides framework and library frames behind a single '… N frames hidden …' line, while always keeping the last frame. It walks the exception chain (`__cause__` and `__context__`, up to five links) and keeps only earlier exceptions that touched project code. Setting `LOG_FULL_TRACEBACKS=true` bypasses all of this and returns the standard traceback.

sections.title: HumanFormatter
sections.explanation: The custom formatter writes `timestamp | LEVEL | logger | req id | message`, with ANSI colours only when enabled. Anything passed as `extra={'details': {...}}` is printed as aligned 'Key : value' lines, with empty values dropped and multi-line values indented. Exception info is appended as the project-focused traceback, and a separator line closes multi-line entries.

sections.title: setup_logging
sections.explanation: Configures the root logger once (the `_log_dir` global makes repeat calls no-ops). It adds a coloured console handler and two `RotatingFileHandler`s (5 MB, 5 backups), with `errors.log` limited to warnings. Uvicorn's own loggers are redirected into this format, and its access log is disabled because the middleware writes a better one. Noisy libraries are raised to WARNING, and if the log folder cannot be created the app keeps running with console logging and a warning.

sections.title: Locating the failing line
sections.explanation: `where_in_code` walks an exception's traceback and keeps the deepest frame that is inside the project and not plumbing. It returns a compact string such as `app/services/incident_service.py:212 in transition()  →  <source line>`, which fills the 'Where' field of error logs.

sections.title: Explaining exceptions in plain English
sections.explanation: `explain_exception` maps exception types to a (what happened, how to fix) pair: MongoDB connection and duplicate-key errors, invalid ObjectIds, SMTP failures (with a Gmail App Password hint), httpx timeouts, JWT errors, Pydantic errors, missing settings (an upper-case `KeyError` key is treated as a missing env variable) and general programming errors. Each optional library import is wrapped in try/except so a missing package cannot break logging. A generic fallback is returned when nothing matches.

sections.title: log_exception
sections.explanation: The single entry point other modules use to log a failure: it attaches the plain-English summary, the error message, caller-supplied details, the code location and the fix hint as the `details` block. `with_traceback=False` lets callers such as the database retry loop log expected, repeated failures without traceback noise.

backend/app/services/seed.py.overview: Idempotent seeding of reference data and demo accounts, called by `init_db` in `db.py` on every startup (Tour Step 2). It upserts categories, IT services with criticality scores, default settings, default SLA policies (including a migration from older defaults) and demo admin, technician and customer users. Most writes use `$setOnInsert`, so restarting the server never overwrites data that users or admins have since changed.

sections.title: Default SLA targets
sections.explanation: `DEFAULT_SLA_TARGETS` maps each priority to (respond, resolve) minutes, matching the project-brief table in the README: P1 5/30 down to P4 4 h/24 h. `OLD_DEFAULT_SLA_TARGETS` is kept only to recognise and upgrade databases seeded with the previous defaults.

sections.title: Categories, services and settings
sections.explanation: Each category and service is upserted by name with `$setOnInsert`, so existing records are left alone and duplicates are never created. Services carry a `criticality` from 1 to 3 that feeds the priority calculation. The settings document is created from `SettingsRepository.DEFAULTS` only if it does not exist; the repository is imported inside the function, which avoids import-time coupling.

sections.title: SLA policies and migration
sections.explanation: For each priority, a global default policy (`service_id: None`) is inserted if missing. A second update matches only policies that still hold exactly the old default values and moves them to the new targets, so policies an admin has edited are untouched. This is a small, safe in-place data migration.

sections.title: Admin account
sections.explanation: The admin email and password come from `ADMIN_EMAIL` and `ADMIN_PASSWORD`, with public defaults. Unlike the other accounts, the password hash, role and active flag are written with `$set` on every startup, so the environment value always wins and a password changed through the app is reset at the next restart.

sections.title: Demo technicians
sections.explanation: Four technicians with distinct skill sets are created, with emails derived from their names. Only the role is enforced with `$set`; the password, skills, capacity and active state use `$setOnInsert`, so password resets and admin deactivations survive restarts, as the inline comment explains. The skill lists give the skill-based assignment strategies something to match against.

sections.title: Demo customers and failure handling
sections.explanation: Seeds three customer accounts, one with a BITS-style email from which a student id and phone number are set. The whole function is wrapped in try/except that logs with `logger.exception` and re-raises, so a seeding failure is visible and is handled by the retry logic in `init_db`.

backend/server.py.overview: The FastAPI entry point (`uvicorn server:app`) and the centre of Tour Step 2. It loads `.env` and configures logging before importing anything else, logs a startup summary of what is configured, starts MongoDB initialisation and the background SLA monitor in the lifespan hook, mounts every router under `/api`, and installs error handling and CORS in a deliberate order.

sections.title: Environment-first imports
sections.explanation: The import order is intentional: `load_dotenv` runs first because modules such as `app.core.db` read environment variables at import time, and `setup_logging()` runs next so that any log output during later imports already uses the project format. Only then are FastAPI, the database handle, the error handling and the ten routers imported.

sections.title: Startup configuration summary
sections.explanation: `log_configuration` writes one readable block showing the MongoDB URL (with credentials redacted), CORS origins and whether Google sign-in, SMTP and Gemini are configured. It then checks `JWT_SECRET`: an error if it is missing (every sign-in would fail) and a warning if it looks like a placeholder or is under 16 characters, because a known secret lets anyone forge admin tokens. A missing SMTP setup is also warned about with a concrete fix.

sections.title: Background SLA loop
sections.explanation: `sla_loop` runs forever, calling `container.sla_monitor.run_once()` and sleeping 60 seconds between passes. Exceptions are caught and logged so one bad pass never kills the loop. The container is imported inside the function, deferring construction of the whole object graph until the loop starts.

sections.title: Lifespan hook
sections.explanation: The `asynccontextmanager` lifespan runs startup code before `yield`: log the configuration, await `init_db()` (which retries until MongoDB is ready) and start the SLA loop as an asyncio task stored on `app.state`. The `finally` block cancels that task, waits for it while suppressing `CancelledError`, and closes the Motor client for a clean shutdown.

sections.title: App, routers and health check
sections.explanation: Creates the FastAPI app with the lifespan and mounts each router module's `router` under the `/api` prefix in one loop. `/api/health` is a lightweight liveness endpoint; the request middleware logs it only at DEBUG to keep logs quiet.

sections.title: Middleware ordering
sections.explanation: Error handling is registered before CORS. In Starlette the middleware added last wraps the others, so CORS is outermost and adds its headers even to 500 responses produced by the logging middleware; without this, browsers would hide the real error behind a generic network error. Origins come from the comma-separated `CORS_ORIGINS`, and `X-Request-ID` is exposed so the frontend can read it.

backend/app/core/container.py.overview: The composition root explained in Tour Step 3. The `Container` class builds every repository, notification channel, observer and service exactly once and passes collaborators in through constructors (hand-written dependency injection). A module-level `container` singleton is created from the shared `db`, and routers and the SLA loop import ready-made objects from it instead of constructing their own.

sections.title: Imports of every collaborator
sections.explanation: The docstring states the file's role. The imports alone show the whole architecture: the event bus from the domain, all MongoDB repositories, the incident, intelligence, notification, observer, SLA and two-factor services. This is the only module that needs to know about all of them.

sections.title: Repositories
sections.explanation: Each repository wraps one MongoDB collection and receives the database handle through its constructor, so a test can pass a different database. `TwoFactorService` is built here too, receiving the security-event repository it logs to: an example of one collaborator being injected into another.

sections.title: Notification channels
sections.explanation: An `SmtpEmailAdapter` (Adapter pattern) is created once and injected into `SmtpEmailChannel`. The `NotificationDispatcher` receives a list of channels: in-app, simulated email and real SMTP. As the comment notes, adding SMS or push later means adding one more channel to this list.

sections.title: Event bus and observers
sections.explanation: This is where the Observer pattern is wired. The audit observer and notification observer subscribe to every event, while `SlaViolationObserver` subscribes only to `SLA_BREACHED` through the optional event-type filter. Services publish events without knowing who listens.

sections.title: Services
sections.explanation: `IncidentService` receives ten collaborators (repositories, intelligence service, event bus and correlation alerts) instead of creating them, which makes its dependencies explicit. `SlaMonitor` receives the incident service as well, so escalation and auto-dispatch reuse the same lifecycle logic.

sections.title: Module-level singleton
sections.explanation: `container = Container(db)` builds the object graph when the module is first imported. Python caches modules, so every `from app.core.container import container` gets the same instance and services are effectively singletons.

backend/app/core/security.py.overview: Authentication and authorization helpers used across the API (Tour Step 4): bcrypt password hashing, JWT creation and decoding for access, refresh and MFA tokens, the safe public view of a user, and the FastAPI dependencies `get_current_user` and `require_roles` that protect routes. Token versions stored on the user let the app invalidate all existing sessions at once.

sections.title: Imports and constants
sections.explanation: Tokens are signed with HS256 using `JWT_SECRET`. MFA tokens, which only prove the password step of a two-step sign-in, last `MFA_TOKEN_MINUTES = 5`. The module reads users directly from the shared `db` handle.

sections.title: Password hashing
sections.explanation: `hash_password` uses bcrypt with a fresh random salt per call, and `verify_password` checks a plaintext against a stored hash. The same helpers are reused in `auth.py` to hash password-reset codes, so even the short-lived codes are never stored in plaintext.

sections.title: Token creation
sections.explanation: Three token types share `_encode`: access tokens (12 hours, carrying user id, email and role), refresh tokens (7 days) and MFA tokens (5 minutes). Each carries a `type` claim, so one kind cannot be used in place of another, and a `tv` token-version claim. Bumping `token_version` on the account makes every older token fail verification, which implements 'sign out of all other devices'.

sections.title: Decoding tokens
sections.explanation: `decode_token` verifies signature and expiry and converts PyJWT errors into 401 `HTTPException`s with distinct 'Token expired' and 'Invalid token' messages. Note that `os.environ['JWT_SECRET']` raises `KeyError` if the secret is missing, which `server.py` warns about at startup.

sections.title: Public user view
sections.explanation: `public_user` builds an explicit allow-list of fields that are safe to send to the browser, so the password hash and TOTP secrets can never leak through it. It also turns the stored `totp_enabled` flag into `two_factor_enabled` and supplies defaults for optional fields.

sections.title: Loading the user behind a token
sections.explanation: `load_user_from_token` decodes the token, checks that its `type` matches what the caller expects, and loads the user by id. An invalid ObjectId is treated as 'user not found' rather than a crash. It rejects deactivated users and tokens whose `tv` does not match the account's current `token_version`, which is the server-side half of session revocation.

sections.title: Current-user dependencies
sections.explanation: `token_from_request` accepts a `Bearer` header, a bare header value or the `access_token` cookie, supporting both the axios client and cookie-based sessions. `get_current_user_doc` returns the raw MongoDB document, while `get_current_user` returns the safe public dict that routes use with `Depends`.

sections.title: Role-based access
sections.explanation: `require_roles(*roles)` is a dependency factory: it returns a new dependency that first resolves `get_current_user` and then checks the role. Failing the check raises `UnauthorizedOperationError`, a domain `ITSMError`, so it goes through the domain error handler, whereas missing or invalid tokens raise a 401 `HTTPException`. Routes write `Depends(require_roles('admin'))` to declare their permissions.

backend/app/models/schemas.py.overview: The Pydantic request models and response-serialization helpers for the API (Tour Step 4). Field constraints such as minimum lengths, numeric ranges and regex patterns make FastAPI reject bad input with a 422 before any route code runs. `serialize` and `clean_doc` convert MongoDB documents to JSON-safe dicts and strip private fields like password hashes and TOTP secrets.

sections.title: Authentication requests
sections.explanation: Models for registration, login, Google sign-in and email password reset. Passwords require at least 8 characters, and the reset code must be exactly six digits through both length limits and a `^\d{6}$` pattern. `GoogleAuthRequest` carries the nonce that `auth.py` compares with the one inside the Google ID token.

sections.title: AI and intelligence payloads
sections.explanation: `AIGeneratedDetails` is the schema that AI-generated incident suggestions must satisfy: bounded title and description lengths, impact and urgency from 1 to 3, a confidence between 0 and 1, and capped list lengths. Validating model output against a strict schema means a malformed AI reply is rejected instead of reaching the form. `SuggestRequest` and `ScopeCheckRequest` back the live suggestion and emergency-scope checks on the report form.

sections.title: Admin-created users
sections.explanation: `CreateUserRequest` is used by admins to create staff accounts, with a role string and a `max_concurrent` capacity limited to 1-50. The mutable `[]` default for `skills` is safe in Pydantic, which copies defaults per instance, unlike a plain Python function default.

sections.title: Incident payloads
sections.explanation: `IncidentCreate` holds the fields used for priority calculation (impact, urgency, business criticality, affected users) plus campus location details. Two flags let a reporter go ahead after a warning: `acknowledge_duplicate` and `confirm_in_scope`. `IncidentUpdate` makes every field optional for PATCH, `TransitionRequest` carries the target status and optional resolution or feedback data, and `AssignRequest` and `NoteInput` are the small payloads for assignment and notes.

sections.title: Catalog and admin configuration
sections.explanation: Inputs for IT services, categories, SLA policies, user edits and global settings. `SlaPolicyInput` restricts priority to `P1`-`P4` with a regex and bounds the minute values. `SettingsUpdate` lets admins switch the assignment and priority strategy by name and tune escalation, correlation and the admin 2FA requirement; every field is optional so partial updates work.

sections.title: Serialization and private fields
sections.explanation: `serialize` recursively converts `ObjectId` to string and `datetime` to ISO format, and drops any key in `PRIVATE_FIELDS` at every nesting level. `clean_doc` renames MongoDB's `_id` to `id` before serializing. Because routers pass documents through these helpers, secrets are stripped centrally rather than per endpoint.

sections.title: Account and security requests
sections.explanation: Models for the second sign-in step, resetting a password with an authenticator code, profile edits, password changes, generic code input and notification preferences. Codes allow up to 20 characters so that longer backup codes fit as well as 6-digit TOTP codes. `current_password` is optional so Google-only accounts can set their first password. `PHONE_PATTERN` is defined here as a shared phone-number regex.

backend/app/routers/auth.py.overview: The `/api/auth` router covering registration, password login with optional two-step verification, email and authenticator-based password resets, Google Workspace sign-in, logout and the current-user endpoint. It relies on the helpers in `security.py`, the schemas in `schemas.py` and services from the container, as described in Tour Step 4. Unlike the incidents router, it reads and writes the `users` and reset collections directly through `db` rather than through repositories.

sections.title: Setup and student id extraction
sections.explanation: Imports the security helpers, request schemas, container, `UserFactory` and domain exceptions. `BITS_EMAIL_DOMAIN` comes from `ALLOWED_EMAIL_DOMAIN`. `extract_student_id` pulls a 6-10 digit number out of a BITS email prefix, falling back to stripping leading letters. A module-level `SmtpEmailAdapter` is created here for reset emails, separate from the one the container builds.

sections.title: Reset email and issuing sessions
sections.explanation: `_send_reset_email` sends the one-time code through the email adapter. `issue` creates access and refresh tokens that include the user's current `token_version`, sets them as `httponly`, `samesite=lax` cookies (secure only when `COOKIE_SECURE=true`), and also returns the access token and public user in the body for the axios client.

sections.title: Registration
sections.explanation: Self-registration is limited to the BITS email domain and duplicate emails raise `AlreadyExistsError`. The user document is built through `UserFactory.create(Role.CUSTOMER, ...)`, so self-registered users are always customers and the domain decides how a role maps to a `User` subclass. Account creation is recorded in the security log before a session is issued.

sections.title: Password login
sections.explanation: A wrong email and a wrong password both raise the same `AuthenticationError`, and failed attempts on real accounts are logged as security events. Deactivated accounts get a 403. If the authenticator is enabled, no session is issued; the response holds a 5-minute MFA token and the allowed methods, which is step one of two-step sign-in.

sections.title: Second sign-in step
sections.explanation: Accepts the MFA token (type `mfa`) plus a code. Token errors are replaced by a friendly 'took too long' message. `container.two_factor.verify` checks the TOTP or backup code and returns which method succeeded. The user is reloaded because verification may change it (for example by using a backup code) before the session is issued with the number of backup codes left.

sections.title: Requesting a reset code
sections.explanation: Returns the same generic message for unknown or deactivated accounts so the endpoint cannot reveal which emails are registered. It limits requests to three per hour using the TTL-indexed `password_reset_requests` collection, and generates the code with `secrets.randbelow`. The email is sent before the code is stored; if sending fails, an `ExternalServiceError` (503) is raised. The stored code is bcrypt-hashed and expires in 10 minutes.

sections.title: Confirming a reset
sections.explanation: Looks up the newest unexpired reset for the email and rejects it after five wrong attempts, counting each failure with `$inc`. On success the password hash is replaced and `token_version` is incremented, which signs out every existing session. All reset records for that email are then deleted and the change is security-logged.

sections.title: Reset with authenticator
sections.explanation: An alternative reset path that needs no email: the user proves possession of their authenticator app instead. Unknown accounts, deactivated accounts and accounts without 2FA all get the same error, avoiding account enumeration. Like the email path, it bumps `token_version` and clears pending email resets.

sections.title: Google sign-in
sections.explanation: The Google ID token is verified server-side with `google-auth` against `GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID`, then issuer and `email_verified` are checked, the nonce is compared in constant time, and the email domain is enforced. Existing users keep their role; only the link flag, display name and student id may be updated, so Google sign-in never elevates privileges. New users are created as customers with an unguessable random password hash so the email/password form cannot be used on Google-only accounts. The credential itself is never logged.

sections.title: Logout and current user
sections.explanation: `logout` just deletes the two cookies; bearer tokens stay valid until they expire unless the token version is bumped. `/me` uses the `get_current_user` dependency and adds `two_factor_required` when the user is an admin and the settings require admin 2FA, which lets the frontend push admins to set up an authenticator.

backend/app/routers/incidents.py.overview: The `/api/incidents` REST surface for the core workflow (Tour Step 4): search, create, detail, state transitions, manual and automatic assignment, notes and updates. It deliberately contains no business logic; each handler validates input through a Pydantic schema, declares authorization with a security dependency, and delegates to the `IncidentService` taken from the container (Step 3), which is explored in Step 5.

sections.title: Router setup
sections.explanation: The router gets its `IncidentService` from the container singleton once at import time, so it never constructs services itself. `STAFF` groups the admin and technician role values for reuse in dependencies. `out` is a thin wrapper over `clean_doc`, so every response is JSON-safe and stripped of private fields.

sections.title: Listing and search
sections.explanation: All search filters (text, status, priority, category, service, technician, SLA status, scope, date range, escalation) arrive as optional query parameters, and `limit` is bounded to 1-500 with `Query`. The handler packs them into a dict and passes them, together with the user, to `service.search`, which applies role-based visibility.

sections.title: Creating an incident
sections.explanation: Returns 201 Created. `require_roles` allows customers and staff, and the `IncidentCreate` schema validates the body before the handler runs. The service handles scope checks, duplicate detection, priority, SLA and assignment.

sections.title: Incident detail
sections.explanation: The one handler with visible orchestration: it loads the incident, calls `service.assert_access` to enforce per-role visibility, and returns a bundle with the incident, the transitions this user may perform (from the State pattern), and the audit trail. Technician recommendations, related incidents and suggested resolutions are only computed for staff, which both hides them from customers and avoids unnecessary work.

sections.title: Transitions and assignment
sections.explanation: `transition` is open to any signed-in user because the State pattern in the service decides which role may make which move. Manual `assign` is limited to staff, and `auto-assign`, which runs the configured assignment strategy, is limited to admins. Both assignment routes load the incident first so a missing id fails before the strategy runs.

sections.title: Notes and updates
sections.explanation: Any signed-in user may add a note; access to the incident is checked inside the service. `PATCH` updates are limited to staff and accept the all-optional `IncidentUpdate` schema, so only the provided fields change.

backend/app/services/incident_service.py.overview: Application service that coordinates the whole incident lifecycle for the incidents router. It owns no business rules itself: it loads documents through repositories, wraps them in the `Incident` aggregate, calls domain methods (classify, apply_priority, assign_to, transition_to), saves only the recorded changes, and publishes `IncidentEvent`s so observers can handle audit and notifications. This is the file Tour Step 5 centres on, and it is where the State, Strategy, Factory and Observer patterns from Steps 6-8 come together.

sections.title: Imports and lookup tables
sections.explanation: The module docstring states the design: IncidentService *has* repositories, an IntelligenceService, settings and an EventBus, and only coordinates them. `OFFLINE_SERVICE_BY_CATEGORY` ties the three physical-support categories (Carpenter, Electrician, Technician) to the service each must use, and `TRANSITION_EVENTS` maps target statuses to more specific event types, falling back to `STATUS_CHANGED`. `_duration` formats minutes as `min`/`h`/`days` for human-readable SLA messages, and `build_location` is a thin backwards-compatibility wrapper around the `Location` value object.

sections.title: Constructor and helpers
sections.explanation: All collaborators are injected through the constructor (they are built once in the composition root), which keeps the service testable. `actor()` turns a raw user dict into the right `User` subclass via `UserFactory`, so access checks can call the polymorphic `can_view`. `allowed_transitions` asks the State object which targets the caller's role may reach and hides `ASSIGNED`, because assignment has its own endpoint. `_publish` builds an immutable event from `incident.snapshot()` and `actor.to_actor()`, unwrapping enum values; `policy()` raises `MissingSlaConfigError` when no SLA matches, and `calculate_priority` picks the strategy named in settings and clamps service criticality to 1..3.

sections.title: Creating an incident
sections.explanation: `create` runs validation in a deliberate order: scope check (unless the reporter confirmed), duplicate detection (unless acknowledged), then service, category and location rules for hostel/offline support. It infers a student ID from the email prefix when none is given. The incident is built by `IncidentFactory`, moved NEW to CLASSIFIED by the system, given a priority and SLA clock, and saved. It then publishes four lifecycle events (created, classified, priority calculated, SLA applied) plus optional duplicate and scope-override notes, checks for correlated reports, and optionally auto-assigns, logging rather than failing if no technician is free.

sections.title: Correlation detection
sections.explanation: `_check_correlation` raises a single 'possible major incident' alert when several incidents hit the same service inside the configured time window. The window and threshold come from settings, the clustering comes from the intelligence service, and an existing alert for the same service inside the window suppresses duplicates. The alert is stored in its own collection and also published as `CORRELATION_DETECTED`, so the notification observer can tell administrators.

sections.title: Role-aware search
sections.explanation: `search` builds a list of MongoDB conditions and combines them with `$and`. Customers only ever see their own reports; technicians see assigned work and the unassigned queue, mirroring `Technician.can_view` so list and detail access agree. Optional filters cover status, priority, SLA status, escalation, date ranges (parsed by `_parse_day`, with an exclusive end date one day later) and a free-text query. The text query is passed through `re.escape` before being used as a case-insensitive regex, which stops user input from being interpreted as regex syntax, and the result size is capped at 500.

sections.title: Manual and automatic assignment
sections.explanation: `assign` checks access, allows technicians only to self-assign, and verifies the target is an active technician. Re-assigning to the same person is a no-op. The real rules (allowed states, workload capacity with the P1 exception) live in `Incident.assign_to` and `Technician.ensure_capacity`; the service only supplies the current open-incident count and records `last_assigned_at`, which the round-robin strategy reads. `auto_assign` looks up the configured `AssignmentStrategy`, ranks technician profiles and delegates to `assign` with the strategy name for the audit message.

sections.title: SLA breach recording
sections.explanation: `record_sla_breaches` publishes `SLA_BREACHED` at most once per deadline kind (response, resolution). It uses the `violations_recorded` list stored on the SLA record to remember what has already been reported, saves that marker first, and only then publishes. The same method is used after transitions and by the background SLA monitor, so the 'once per deadline' guarantee holds no matter which path notices the breach.

sections.title: State transitions
sections.explanation: `transition` validates the requested status, refuses `ASSIGNED` (assignment has its own endpoint) and requires a resolution summary for RESOLVED. `incident.transition_to` delegates to the State pattern, which raises if the move or role is not allowed. Side effects depend on the target: acknowledge stops the response clock, resolve stores a Resolution, a RESOLVED to IN_PROGRESS move is treated as a reopen with its own event, and close records feedback. The event type and description are chosen afterwards, and SLA breaches are re-checked before returning the fresh document.

sections.title: Notes and detail updates
sections.explanation: `add_note` refuses notes on closed incidents and generates the note ID with `ObjectId()`; the repository appends new notes with `$push` instead of overwriting the array. `update` applies only the non-null fields, and if any priority input (impact, urgency, criticality, affected users) changed it recalculates priority with the current strategy and re-applies the SLA policy, looking up the service criticality if the document lacks it. Two events can result: `INCIDENT_UPDATED` listing the changed fields, and `PRIORITY_CHANGED` when the priority actually moved.

backend/app/domain/enums.py.overview: Defines the shared vocabularies used across the backend: user roles, the nine incident statuses, priorities P1-P4 and SLA statuses. Every enum subclasses `str`, so values compare equal to the plain strings stored in MongoDB and serialise to JSON without conversion. It supports Tour Step 6, where the state machine and domain model are built on these values.

sections.title: String-backed enums
sections.explanation: Each class inherits from both `str` and `Enum`, which means `Role.ADMIN == 'admin'` is true and the values can be written straight into documents and API responses. `Role.SYSTEM` represents automation (SLA monitor, auto-assignment) rather than a human account. `IncidentStatus` lists the full lifecycle from NEW to CLOSED that `state.py` turns into a state machine, and `SlaStatus` holds the four values the SLA evaluator produces. The compact one-line style with semicolons is legal Python but unusual; it trades readability for brevity.

sections.title: Open statuses list
sections.explanation: `OPEN_STATUSES` is a list of plain string values for every status before RESOLVED. It is used in MongoDB `$in` queries (for example to count a technician's open workload in the repository) and by `Incident.is_open`. Note that RESOLVED and VERIFIED are not counted as open, so a resolved incident no longer counts against a technician's capacity.

backend/app/domain/exceptions.py.overview: The custom exception hierarchy for business-rule failures. Every error derives from `ITSMError` and carries its own HTTP status code, so routers and services simply raise domain exceptions and a single handler in `app/core/error_handling.py` converts them to JSON responses. It is part of the domain layer covered in Tour Step 6, and these exceptions are raised throughout the State pattern, the strategies and the IncidentService.

sections.title: Base ITSMError
sections.explanation: `ITSMError` stores a human-readable `message` and an `extra` dict of keyword arguments that the error handler adds to the JSON body. The default `status_code` is 400, and subclasses override it as a class attribute. This is how, for example, the admin router attaches `code='2fa_required'` and `OutOfScopeError` carries the scope assessment back to the client.

sections.title: Input and authentication errors
sections.explanation: These cover bad requests and access problems: `InvalidInputError` (422), `InvalidCodeError` (a 422 for wrong one-time codes), `TooManyAttemptsError` (429), `AuthenticationError` (401) and `UnauthorizedOperationError` (403). Because `InvalidCodeError` subclasses `InvalidInputError`, it inherits the 422 status code while still being catchable on its own.

sections.title: Lookup and lifecycle conflicts
sections.explanation: `ResourceNotFoundError` (404) has a `ServiceNotFoundError` subclass, so callers can catch either level. The 409 Conflict family covers lifecycle and data clashes: illegal state transitions, no available technician, duplicates, existing names and configuration still in use. `WorkloadExceededError` subclasses `TechnicianUnavailableError`, which lets `create` catch the broader type when auto-assignment fails for any capacity-related reason.

sections.title: Scope, configuration and infrastructure errors
sections.explanation: `OutOfScopeError` (422) is raised when a report is not an IT or facilities issue. `MissingSlaConfigError` uses 500 because a missing SLA policy is a server configuration problem, not a user mistake. `ExternalServiceError` and `DatabaseUnavailableError` use 503 to signal temporary unavailability of SMTP, Google, AI or MongoDB.

backend/app/domain/models.py.overview: The object-oriented core of the project. It defines an abstract `User` hierarchy with polymorphic access rules, immutable catalog value objects, the parts an incident is composed of, and the `Incident` aggregate root that is the only way incident documents are changed. Tour Step 6 calls this file the OOP heart of the system; the IncidentService from Step 5 calls these methods, and the repository from Step 9 persists the changes they record.

sections.title: Design notes and imports
sections.explanation: The docstring includes a class diagram and explains the rules the file follows: inheritance only for real is-a relationships, composition for incident parts, private fields behind read-only properties, and state changes only through rule-enforcing methods. It also explains the persistence contract: classes convert to and from MongoDB documents, and callers save `changes()` instead of editing documents directly.

sections.title: Abstract User base class
sections.explanation: `User` is an `ABC` that validates and normalises name, email and phone in its constructor and stores them in underscore-prefixed fields. The read-only properties are written as `property(lambda self: ...)` one-liners. `can_view` is abstract, so each subclass must define its own access rule. `to_doc` uses the template-method hook `_extra_fields` so subclasses can add role-specific fields, and `to_actor` produces the small dict that goes into events and audit records.

sections.title: Concrete user roles
sections.explanation: Each subclass fixes its `role` and implements `can_view` differently: an `Employee` sees only incidents it reported, a `Technician` sees unassigned, own or still-new incidents, and an `Administrator` and the `SystemActor` see everything. `Technician` validates `max_concurrent` against `MAX_CAPACITY`, removes duplicate skills while keeping order via `dict.fromkeys`, and `ensure_capacity` lets P1 incidents exceed the workload limit. `SYSTEM` is a module-level singleton used as the actor for automated actions.

sections.title: UserFactory
sections.explanation: The Factory pattern picks the right `User` subclass for a role string. `create` validates the role and email format, and always returns the shared `SYSTEM` instance for the system role. `from_doc` accepts either a MongoDB document (`_id`) or the API's public user dict (`id`), fills safe defaults for missing name or email, and clamps `max_concurrent` so older or malformed records still load.

sections.title: Catalog value objects
sections.explanation: `ItService` and `SlaPolicy` are frozen dataclasses, meaning immutable value objects built from documents with `from_doc`. `ItService.criticality` (1 to 3) feeds into the weighted priority strategy. `SlaPolicy.start_clock` delegates to `build_sla` in `sla.py` to compute response and resolution deadlines from the incident's creation time.

sections.title: Incident parts
sections.explanation: `Location`, `Note`, `Resolution` and `Closure` are frozen dataclasses composed into an incident. Each validates itself in `__post_init__`: an allowed location type, a non-empty resolution summary, a rating from 1 to 5. `Location.formatted` builds a readable place string for each of the online, hostel and academics cases, and `to_doc` stores that string next to the raw fields so it can be searched and displayed without recomputing it.

sections.title: Incident aggregate: state and change tracking
sections.explanation: `Incident` wraps a copy of the stored document and keeps the matching State object from `StateFactory`. Fields are exposed through read-only properties. Every modification goes through `_set`, which updates the document and also records the key in `_changes`, so the repository can write only changed fields with `$set`. New notes are tracked separately so they can be appended with `$push`, and `mark_saved` clears both after persistence. `snapshot` returns the compact summary that events carry.

sections.title: Incident aggregate: behaviour
sections.explanation: These methods enforce the business rules. `transition_to` delegates to the current State object, which raises on illegal moves. `apply_priority` restarts the SLA clock only when the priority changes, but keeps `responded_at`, `resolved_at` and `violations_recorded` from the previous record. `assign_to` allows (re)assignment only from CLASSIFIED or ASSIGNED and checks technician capacity. Other methods handle acknowledging, resolving, reopening, closing, notes, detail edits (rebuilding `Location` when location fields change), SLA refresh, violation markers and escalation history.

sections.title: IncidentFactory
sections.explanation: The factory builds a brand-new incident document in the NEW state with every field set explicitly, including `None` placeholders for priority, SLA, resolution and closure. It enforces a minimum title length and copies service and reporter details onto the incident (a deliberate denormalisation for fast listing and search). The IncidentService then immediately classifies the incident and applies priority before saving.

backend/app/domain/state.py.overview: Implements the State pattern for the incident lifecycle. Each status has its own state class that declares which target statuses are reachable and which roles may trigger each move, and a registry-based factory returns the shared state instance for a status. `Incident.transition_to` in models.py delegates here, which is why illegal moves are rejected consistently everywhere (Tour Step 6).

sections.title: IncidentState base class
sections.explanation: The base class holds a `transitions` dict that maps each target status to the set of roles allowed to perform the move. `allowed_targets(role)` powers the role-specific action buttons in the UI, and `is_terminal` is true when no transitions remain. `transition` distinguishes two failure modes: a target that is not reachable at all raises `InvalidStateTransitionError` (409), while a reachable target that the role may not trigger raises `UnauthorizedOperationError` (403).

sections.title: Concrete lifecycle states
sections.explanation: Each subclass is a single line declaring its name and transition table, so the whole lifecycle can be read at a glance: NEW, CLASSIFIED, ASSIGNED, ACKNOWLEDGED, IN_PROGRESS, then either PENDING_INFO (back to IN_PROGRESS) or RESOLVED, and finally VERIFIED and CLOSED. Notable rules: only the customer or an admin can verify or reopen a resolved incident, customers can move PENDING_INFO back to IN_PROGRESS after providing info, and `ClosedState` has an empty table, which makes it terminal.

sections.title: StateFactory registry
sections.explanation: `StateFactory` builds one instance of every state class at import time and indexes them by status. The states hold no per-incident data, so sharing these instances is safe (they act like flyweights). `get` accepts either an enum or a raw string, because `S(status)` normalises the string stored in MongoDB.

backend/app/domain/strategies.py.overview: Implements the Strategy pattern for the two decisions IncidentService delegates: calculating priority and choosing a technician. Each algorithm is a separate class behind an abstract interface, and factories look them up by the key stored in the admin settings, so the algorithm can be changed at runtime without editing the service. This is the core of Tour Step 7, together with the admin router that exposes the choice.

sections.title: Priority inputs and results
sections.explanation: `PriorityInput` is a dataclass that validates its own ranges in `__post_init__`: impact, urgency and both criticalities must be 1 to 3, and affected users at least 1. `PriorityResult` carries the priority, numeric score, strategy key and a human-readable explanation that ends up in the audit trail. `PriorityStrategy` is the abstract interface, with `key`, `name` and `description` class attributes that describe it to the admin UI.

sections.title: Priority strategies and factory
sections.explanation: `MatrixPriorityStrategy` is the classic ITIL impact times urgency grid. `WeightedScorePriorityStrategy` multiplies by the higher of business and service criticality and adds a stepped bonus for many affected users, so an outage of a critical service rises in priority even if the reporter underrates it. `PriorityStrategyFactory` keeps a registry keyed by `key` and falls back to the `weighted` default for unknown names; `describe` feeds the strategy picker in the admin settings.

sections.title: Technician profiles and ranking types
sections.explanation: `TechnicianProfile` is a read model assembled by the intelligence service: skills, current workload, category and service experience, average resolution time and last assignment time. `has_capacity` compares open incidents to the technician's limit. `Ranked` wraps a profile with a score and a per-factor breakdown, which only the smart strategy produces.

sections.title: AssignmentStrategy template method
sections.explanation: `select` is a template method shared by all strategies: subclasses only implement `rank`. It filters to technicians with free capacity, but for P1 incidents falls back to the full ranked list so critical work is never blocked by capacity, and raises `TechnicianUnavailableError` otherwise. The `tech` lambda unwraps `Ranked` objects with `getattr(r, 'technician', r)`, so `rank` may return either plain profiles or `Ranked` wrappers.

sections.title: Simple ranking strategies
sections.explanation: These strategies each rank with a single sort key. Skill-based prefers a category match, then capacity, then lighter load; load-balanced uses capacity and open count only. Round robin sorts ascending by `last_assigned_at`, treating 'never assigned' as the earliest timezone-aware datetime so those technicians go first. Experience-based sums category and service resolutions and breaks ties by faster average resolution, treating a missing average as very slow.

sections.title: Smart and priority-based strategies
sections.explanation: `SmartRecommendationStrategy` computes a weighted score from five normalised factors (skill 35%, free capacity 25%, category experience 20%, service experience 10%, speed 10%) and keeps the breakdown so the UI can explain the recommendation. `PriorityBasedStrategy` is a composite: for P1/P2 it reuses the experience strategy, ranking skilled technicians before everyone else, and for P3/P4 it delegates to load balancing. This shows strategies being reused inside other strategies.

sections.title: AssignmentStrategyFactory
sections.explanation: Mirrors the priority factory: a registry keyed by each class's `key`, a `smart` default for unknown names, and `describe` for the admin UI. Because the admin router validates new settings against `registry`, adding a strategy class here automatically makes it selectable.

backend/app/routers/admin.py.overview: FastAPI router for administrator and IT-manager endpoints under `/admin`: user and technician management, IT services, categories, SLA policies, strategy and automation settings, the audit log and the SLA violation register. Its role in Tour Step 7 is the settings endpoints, which let an admin switch the priority and assignment strategies at runtime by name. Every endpoint depends on the `admin` guard, and errors are raised as domain exceptions for the central error handler.

sections.title: Router setup and admin guard
sections.explanation: The router obtains all repositories from the shared `container` (aliased as `c`). The `admin` dependency builds on `require_roles(Role.ADMIN)` and additionally enforces the optional 'require admin 2FA' setting, raising an `UnauthorizedOperationError` with `code='2fa_required'` so the frontend can send the admin to the security page. Reusing this one dependency on every route keeps authorisation consistent.

sections.title: User and technician management
sections.explanation: Admins may create only admin or technician accounts (customers sign up themselves), and duplicate emails raise `AlreadyExistsError`. Creation and updates both go through `UserFactory`, so the same domain validation applies; `update_user` validates by building a throwaway domain object from the merged document. Password hashes are removed before responses, admins cannot deactivate themselves, and `reset-2fa` clears all authenticator fields with `$unset` and records a security event.

sections.title: IT services and categories
sections.explanation: Listings include an `incident_count` per item so the UI can show which entries are in use. Names must be unique. Renaming a service also updates the denormalised `service_name` on existing incidents with `update_many`. Deletion is refused with `ResourceInUseError` while incidents still reference the service or category, and deleting a service also removes its service-specific SLA policies.

sections.title: SLA policy management
sections.explanation: `_validate_policy` checks that the resolution target is not shorter than the response target, that a referenced service exists, and that only one policy exists per priority and service pair. Policies with `service_id` of `None` are the per-priority defaults: they cannot change priority or become service-specific, and they cannot be deleted, because `IncidentService.policy` relies on a default always being present.

sections.title: Strategy and automation settings
sections.explanation: This is the runtime switch for the Strategy pattern from Tour Step 7. `GET /settings` returns the current settings together with the factories' `describe()` output, so the UI lists available algorithms without hard-coding them. `PUT /settings` validates strategy names against the factory registries and escalation priorities against the `Priority` enum, and refuses to enable mandatory admin 2FA for an admin who has not set it up, which would otherwise lock them out.

sections.title: Audit log and SLA violations
sections.explanation: The audit endpoint builds a MongoDB filter from optional incident, action, actor and date parameters; free-text values are passed through `re.escape` before being used in regex filters. It reuses `IncidentService._parse_day` for date parsing through a local import, and the date range end is exclusive (one day later). The SLA violation register returns records written by `SlaViolationObserver`, newest first.

backend/app/domain/events.py.overview: Defines the Observer pattern infrastructure: the event type enum, the immutable `IncidentEvent`, the `EventObserver` interface and the `EventBus` subject. IncidentService only publishes what happened; observers decide how to react (audit trail, notifications, SLA violation register). This is the foundation of Tour Step 8 and means new reactions can be added without changing the service.

sections.title: Module purpose and event types
sections.explanation: The docstring describes the decoupling: adding an SMS observer, for example, means one new class plus one `subscribe` call. `EventType` is a `str` enum covering every lifecycle moment, from creation, classification and SLA application through assignment, status changes, notes, SLA risk and breach, escalation and correlation. These values are also stored as the `action` field of audit records.

sections.title: IncidentEvent
sections.explanation: A frozen dataclass, so an event cannot be changed after publication. It carries a snapshot of the incident and actor as plain dicts rather than live domain objects, which keeps observers from mutating the aggregate and makes events easy to store. The timestamp is filled by `default_factory` at creation time, and `data` holds event-specific extras such as the SLA kind or resolution summary.

sections.title: Observer interface and EventBus
sections.explanation: `EventObserver` defines a single async `on_event` method. `EventBus.subscribe` can optionally restrict an observer to a set of event types (stored as a `frozenset`, or `None` for all events). `publish` calls the matching observers in order and catches every exception, logging it as a warning, so that a failing observer such as a broken email server can never break the user's request.

backend/app/services/email.py.overview: A small synchronous helper that sends one plain-text email through the SMTP account configured in environment variables. It is the external dependency that `SmtpEmailAdapter` in notifications.py wraps, so the rest of the notification system never touches `smtplib` directly (Tour Step 8).

sections.title: SMTP send helper
sections.explanation: Configuration is read from `SMTP_*` environment variables at call time, and the sender address falls back to the username. Missing configuration raises a `RuntimeError`, which the SMTP channel catches and records as a failed email log entry. The message is built with `EmailMessage` and sent over STARTTLS with a 15-second timeout. Because `smtplib` is blocking, the adapter runs this function with `asyncio.to_thread` instead of calling it directly from async code.

backend/app/services/notifications.py.overview: Implements notification delivery: a `Notification` value object, an Adapter around the blocking email helper, several delivery channels (in-app, simulated email log, real SMTP email) and a dispatcher that fans one notification out to many recipients over every channel that supports it. `NotificationObserver` from observers.py decides who should hear about an event, and this module handles how it is delivered (Tour Step 8).

sections.title: Overview and Notification value object
sections.explanation: The docstring shows the class layout and states the extension point: SMS or push notifications would be one more `NotificationChannel` subclass passed to the dispatcher. `Notification` is a frozen dataclass holding the in-app title and message, a `kind` used for channel filtering, the incident reference, and optional email-specific subject and body that override the defaults.

sections.title: EmailSender adapter
sections.explanation: `EmailSender` is the interface the app expects from any email provider: an async `send` and `is_configured`. `SmtpEmailAdapter` adapts the synchronous `send_email` function by running it in a worker thread with `asyncio.to_thread`, so a slow SMTP server does not block the event loop. Swapping to an HTTP email API would mean writing another adapter class.

sections.title: Channel interface, in-app and simulated email
sections.explanation: `NotificationChannel.supports` defaults to true, and channels override it to opt out. `InAppChannel` writes an unread document into `notifications`, which backs the bell icon. `wants_email` respects the user's email preference but always lets `security` notifications through. `SimulatedEmailChannel` records a 'queued' entry in `email_logs`, which provides a visible email trail even when no SMTP server is configured.

sections.title: SMTP email channel
sections.explanation: Real email is limited to a few event kinds by default (resolved, SLA breached, escalation, security) to avoid flooding inboxes. `supports` also requires an email address, the user's consent and a configured sender. Success and failure are both logged to `email_logs`; on failure the error is truncated to 500 characters and the log notes that the in-app notification was still delivered.

sections.title: NotificationDispatcher
sections.explanation: `notify` skips empty recipients, the `system` pseudo-user and anyone already notified, so passing overlapping lists (for example technician, reporter and all admins) never produces duplicates. Each channel send is wrapped in its own try/except, so one failing channel does not stop the others or other recipients.

backend/app/services/observers.py.overview: Concrete observers subscribed to the EventBus. One writes every event to the audit trail, one records SLA breaches in a dedicated violation register, and one decides who should be notified about each event type and what they are told. Together they are the side-effect layer described in Tour Step 8, kept separate from IncidentService.

sections.title: AuditObserver
sections.explanation: Turns each `IncidentEvent` into an audit document that flattens incident and actor fields (number, actor name and role, previous and new state, extra data, timestamp). Because it receives every event, the audit log becomes the complete incident history shown on the detail page and searched by the admin audit endpoint.

sections.title: SlaViolationObserver
sections.explanation: Stores each SLA breach as a separate document including priority, service, assignee, which deadline was missed and when. The observer itself does not filter by type; the subscription in the composition root is expected to limit it to `SLA_BREACHED` events, which is why it can read `kind` and `due_at` from `e.data` directly.

sections.title: NotificationObserver recipient lookup
sections.explanation: Recipients are resolved lazily from the user repository. `_user` returns `None` for the system actor, missing users and inactive accounts, so deactivated users stop receiving notifications without extra checks. Each recipient dict includes the `email_notifications` preference that the email channels use.

sections.title: Event-to-notification rules
sections.explanation: `on_event` is a dispatch table written as an if/elif chain on the event type. A few short lambdas reduce repetition: `not_actor` avoids notifying people about their own actions, and `msg` builds a `Notification` with the incident reference. Rules are role-specific: reporters hear about creation, assignment, info requests and resolution (with a full email body), technicians about assignments and notes, and admins about new P1 incidents, SLA breaches and correlated outages. SLA-at-risk warnings go to the assignee or, if none, to the admins.

backend/app/repositories.py.overview: Holds all MongoDB access behind the Repository pattern. A generic `MongoRepository` supplies CRUD for one collection, and subclasses add collection-specific queries for incidents, users, catalog items, SLA policies, audit logs, security events, notifications, violations, correlation alerts and settings. Services and observers talk only to these classes, which is the separation Tour Step 9 describes.

sections.title: Module purpose and ObjectId helper
sections.explanation: The docstring explains the goal: the database could be swapped by writing new repository classes without touching business logic. `to_object_id` converts strings to `ObjectId` and turns a malformed ID into `ResourceNotFoundError` instead of a 500 error, so a bad URL parameter produces a clean 404.

sections.title: Generic MongoRepository
sections.explanation: Subclasses set only `collection_name` and `entity_name`; the base class provides `get`, `find` (with optional sort, limit and projection), `count`, `add`, `update` and `delete`. Missing records raise `ResourceNotFoundError` with a message built from the entity name. `add` writes the generated `_id` back onto the passed dict, and `update` returns the fresh document after the `$set`.

sections.title: IncidentRepository
sections.explanation: `get` accepts either a Mongo ID or a human-readable number such as `INC-00012`. `next_number` uses an atomic `find_one_and_update` with `$inc` and `upsert` on a counters collection, so concurrent creations never receive the same number. `save_changes` is the persistence half of the aggregate's change tracking: it `$set`s only changed fields, `$push`es new notes with `$each` so existing notes are never overwritten, then calls `mark_saved`. `open_count_for` can exclude the current incident when checking capacity.

sections.title: UserRepository
sections.explanation: Emails are normalised to lowercase before lookup, matching how `User` stores them. `active_technicians` and `active_admins` support assignment and notifications. `list_public` uses a projection that excludes `PRIVATE_FIELDS` (password hash and TOTP secrets) at query level, so sensitive fields never reach the admin user list.

sections.title: Catalog and SLA policy repositories
sections.explanation: Services and categories add a `by_name` lookup used for uniqueness checks. `SlaPolicyRepository.find_for` implements the SLA resolution rule: a policy specific to the service and priority wins, otherwise the default policy for that priority (`service_id` of `None`) is used.

sections.title: Audit and security event repositories
sections.explanation: `AuditRepository.for_incident` returns an incident's history oldest first, already cleaned for the API. `SecurityEventRepository.record` captures sign-ins and account changes along with client IP and user agent; `_client` prefers the first `X-Forwarded-For` address (useful behind a proxy) and truncates the user agent to 300 characters.

sections.title: Simple collection repositories
sections.explanation: Notifications, SLA violations and correlation alerts need only the inherited CRUD operations, so each subclass just names its collection. This shows the benefit of the generic base: a new collection costs three lines.

sections.title: SettingsRepository
sections.explanation: System settings live in a single document with the fixed ID `system`. `get_settings` merges stored values over `DEFAULTS`, so a fresh database still works and newly added settings get sensible defaults without a migration. `update_settings` upserts with `$set` and returns the merged result. These are the values the admin settings endpoint edits and that IncidentService reads to choose strategies.

backend/app/domain/campus.py.overview: Reference data and text-parsing rules specific to the BITS Pilani Hyderabad campus. It lists the hostels and academic blocks, and exposes two pure functions that read a location and a business-criticality level out of a free-text report. IntelligenceService.generate_incident_details (tour step 10) uses them to autofill the report form from the student's own words, so the location survives even if the AI shortened the description.

sections.title: Campus reference lists
sections.explanation: `HOSTELS` and `ACADEMIC_BLOCKS` are the canonical display names for campus places. The parsing functions below always return these exact strings, which is why the regexes map matches back onto formatted names such as `'NAB (New Academic Block)'` instead of returning the raw text the student typed.

sections.title: Location and keyword regexes
sections.explanation: Every pattern is compiled once at import time. `_BLOCK_RX` is an ordered list of `(regex, formatter)` pairs, so each rule can build its own canonical name from the match (for example `Block D` from `d-block` or `blk d`). `_ROOM_RX` has two layers: a strict `LTC-101` / `D-204` style first, then a looser `room 12`, `lab 3` style. `CRITICAL_WORDS` and `IMPORTANT_WORDS` hold the vocabulary that `estimate_criticality` uses to score urgency.

sections.title: extract_location
sections.explanation: Lowercases the text and fills a fixed-shape dict. Hostels are checked before academic blocks, and the `else` branch means a report gets at most one location type. The first block rule that matches wins, so the order of `_BLOCK_RX` decides ties. The room number is extracted on its own, so a room can be found even when no hostel or block was named. Because the dict always has the same keys, callers can check `location['type']` without guarding for missing keys.

sections.title: estimate_criticality
sections.explanation: A three-level heuristic that matches the `business_criticality` scale used in the Gemini prompt: 3 for exams, payments and deadlines, 2 for coursework, 1 otherwise. Critical words are checked first, so a report that mentions both an exam and an assignment scores 3. The service only uses this value when the AI did not supply one.

backend/app/domain/scope.py.overview: Decides whether a report belongs at the IT/facilities help desk. Medical emergencies, mental-health crises, fire, electrical danger, security incidents, pests and other non-IT matters are redirected to the right campus or national contacts instead of becoming tickets. Two layers make the decision: a deterministic keyword classifier and an optional AI opinion. They are merged with a safety-first rule, so the rules' life-safety verdict always wins. This file is the scope detection half of tour step 10.

sections.title: Design rationale docstring
sections.explanation: The module docstring sets out the policy: rules always run because the demo may have no AI access, the AI is consulted when configured, and a possible life-safety match from the rules overrides the AI. The stated trade-off is that a false alarm costs one click, while a missed emergency could cost much more. That asymmetry explains why the code below favours over-detection.

sections.title: Contacts and ScopeKind
sections.explanation: `Contact` is a frozen dataclass, so the phone directory cannot be changed by accident at runtime. `ScopeKind` subclasses both `str` and `Enum`, which lets values serialise directly to JSON and compare equal to plain strings coming from the AI. The two sets `IN_SCOPE` and `LIFE_SAFETY` are what the rest of the module actually branches on. Security and pest are out of scope but not life-safety.

sections.title: Guidance per kind
sections.explanation: A lookup table from each out-of-scope kind to the title, message and ordered contact list shown to the student. The `emergency` flag drives the urgent banner in the frontend's NewIncident form. The short aliases `C` and `N` keep the table readable. The mental-health entry puts the Tele-MANAS helpline first and uses supportive wording.

sections.title: ScopeAssessment result
sections.explanation: The value object returned by every classifier. The `for_kind` factory fills in guidance automatically for out-of-scope kinds, so callers never assemble titles or contacts by hand. In-scope results carry no guidance. `to_dict` converts the enum to its string value for the JSON API. `source` records whether the verdict came from 'rules', 'ai' or 'ai+rules'.

sections.title: Text normalisation helpers
sections.explanation: `normalise` applies Unicode NFKC folding, lowercases, unifies curly apostrophes and collapses whitespace, so the regexes see one consistent form. `_deleet` reverses common obfuscation such as 'su1c1de' or spaced-out letters, and keeps Devanagari and Telugu characters. It is used only as a fallback for crisis terms. `W` and `E` are lookaround word boundaries, used instead of `\b` so that matching stays predictable around apostrophes and non-ASCII text.

sections.title: IT idioms to strip
sections.explanation: Phrases that sound alarming but are everyday IT language ('kill the process', 'dead pixel', 'firewall', 'stolen password', 'python', 'killing me') are removed before any emergency rule runs. This is the main defence against false positives. For example, 'fire' in 'Fire TV' or 'theft' in 'stolen credentials' would otherwise trigger the fire or security guidance.

sections.title: Rule tables and priority
