sections.explanation: `RULES` maps each non-IT kind to its regex list, including Hindi and Telugu terms for self-harm. `IT_SIGNALS` detects IT or facilities vocabulary. It is used only to soften the low-stakes `OTHER` category, so 'my marks on the ERP portal' stays an IT ticket. `PRIORITY` orders the kinds from most to least severe, so when several kinds match, the most serious one is reported.

sections.title: RuleBasedScopeClassifier
sections.explanation: Normalises title and description together, strips IT idioms, then walks `PRIORITY`. For mental health it falls back to the de-leeted compact text. Life-safety kinds return immediately. Security and pest also return immediately, because cyber phrasing was already stripped. `OTHER` is returned only when no IT context is present. If nothing matches, the report is classified as IT. The classifier needs no I/O, so it can run on every keystroke.

sections.title: AI parsing and safety-first merge
sections.explanation: `parse_ai_kind` tolerates loose AI output by normalising the string, trying the enum, then an alias table. It returns `None` when the answer is unusable. `combine` encodes the safety rule. If the rules found a life-safety kind, that kind wins and the source is marked 'ai+rules' only when the AI agreed. If the AI gave no answer, the rules verdict stands. Otherwise the AI's kind is used, and the rule matches are kept only when both sides agree.

backend/app/routers/intelligence.py.overview: A thin FastAPI router that exposes the IntelligenceService under `/api/intelligence`. Every endpoint authenticates the caller. Analysis that reveals other people's incidents (duplicates, recommendations, correlations) is restricted to administrators and technicians. All behaviour lives in the service obtained from the DI container, which matches the layering shown in tour step 10.

sections.title: Router setup
sections.explanation: The router takes its service from the module-level `container` (tour step 3) instead of building one, so it shares the same IntelligenceService and database handle as the rest of the app. `STAFF` is a tuple of role values that is unpacked into `require_roles(*STAFF)` below.

sections.title: Classification endpoints
sections.explanation: `/classify` and `/generate-incident` are open to any authenticated user, students included, because they feed the report form. `/generate-incident` declares `response_model=AIGeneratedDetails`, so FastAPI validates the service's dict against the schema. That is why the service carefully pads titles and descriptions to their minimum lengths.

sections.title: Staff-only analysis
sections.explanation: Duplicate search, technician recommendation and correlation clusters reveal other incidents, so they require the admin or technician role. `/recommend/{iid}` also calls `assert_access` on the incident service, adding an object-level check on top of the role check. `/correlations` reads its window and threshold from the admin-editable settings document, so administrators can tune them without redeploying.

sections.title: Scope check and autofill
sections.explanation: `/scope` returns the `ScopeAssessment` as a dict. The frontend calls it with `use_ai=false` while the student types (instant, rules only) and with `use_ai=true` before submitting. `/suggest` is synchronous on the service side because it is pure keyword ranking with no database or network access.

backend/app/services/intelligence.py.overview: The 'smart' layer of BITS reports. It contains concept-based duplicate detection, keyword rule tables for categories and services, a Gemini adapter that treats the model's reply as untrusted input, and the IntelligenceService facade. The facade combines these pieces with the scope rules, campus parsing and strategy-based technician ranking. Every AI path falls back to deterministic heuristics, so the app works without an API key. This is the core file of tour step 10.

sections.title: Imports and tokenising helpers
sections.explanation: `tokens` produces lowercase alphanumeric words longer than two characters, minus a stop list. It is used for similarity in resolution suggestions and incident correlation. `keyword_count` matches whole words with optional plural endings, using explicit lookarounds. As its docstring explains, this stops 'ui' matching 'building' or 'fire' matching 'firewall'.

sections.title: Concept normalisation for duplicates
sections.explanation: Before comparing reports, `concepts` rewrites negated phrases such as "can't connect" into a single FAILURE marker, stems simple suffixes with `_stem`, and maps synonyms onto shared concepts (pay, UPI and transaction all become 'payment'). `CONCEPT_WEIGHTS` gives FAILURE only 0.3, because nearly every report says something is broken. `jaccard` and `dice` are weighted set-similarity measures built on `_weight`.

sections.title: DuplicateDetector
sections.explanation: Scores a candidate as 0.75 times the better of title-to-title Dice and whole-report Jaccard, plus 0.25 when both reports name the same service. Dice is used for titles because short titles carry the most signal. Candidates at or above `THRESHOLD = 0.45` are returned sorted by score, capped at `limit`. The detector is pure: database access happens in `find_duplicates`.

sections.title: Keyword rule tables
sections.explanation: `RULES` covers the online IT categories, `OFFLINE_RULES` covers room-repair categories (electrician, carpenter, technician), and `SERVICE_RULES` maps text to catalogue services. `STRONG_KEYWORDS` weights distinctive words such as 'phishing' or 'vpn' above generic ones. `GEMINI_STATUS_HINTS` turns HTTP status codes into concrete fix-it messages for the logs.

sections.title: Classifier interface and Gemini prompt
sections.explanation: `IncidentClassifier` is the abstraction, and `GeminiAdapter` applies the Adapter pattern to Google's REST API. The model name is checked against a strict regex because it is placed in the URL. `from_env` returns `None` when no key is set, which is the signal to use heuristics. The `transport` argument lets tests inject an `httpx.MockTransport`. The prompt wraps the report in `<report>` tags and tells the model to treat it as data, which is a prompt-injection defence. `_clean_input` strips control characters and caps the length.

sections.title: Reply validation and API call
sections.explanation: The validators `_int`, `_text` and `_extract_json` never trust the model. They clamp numbers, map words like 'high' to 3, reject nested objects, strip markdown fences and fall back to the outermost `{...}`. `_normalise` keeps a category only if it matches an allowed one, case-insensitively. `classify` sends the API key in a header rather than the URL so it cannot leak into logs, and retries once on 5xx responses. Every failure path logs a specific reason and returns `None`, so the caller falls back to keyword classification.

sections.title: IntelligenceService: suggest, scope, classify
sections.explanation: The `classifier_factory` dependency is called on each use, so a key added to the environment takes effect without a restart, and tests can substitute fakes. `suggest` ranks only the category and service names the form currently allows. `assess_scope` always runs the rules and skips the AI entirely when the rules detect a life-safety case, so an emergency response never waits on the network. `classify` keeps Gemini's fields but fills in the category from keywords when Gemini named one that does not exist.

sections.title: Heuristic classification fallback
sections.explanation: Picks the category with the most keyword hits, then puts the report into one of three severity bands (campus-critical, moderate or individual) based on outage and scale words. Each band sets impact, urgency, score, affected users and canned root-cause and action text. The result has the same shape as Gemini's normalised output, with `source: 'heuristic'`, so callers handle both the same way.

sections.title: generate_incident_details
sections.explanation: Produces editable form suggestions and never creates an incident. Scope is checked first, reusing Gemini's scope answer when available. Out-of-scope reports come back with the student's words untouched plus guidance. For in-scope reports it derives priority from the impact and urgency pair, raises urgency in keyword mode for failure words or high criticality, extracts the location from the original text, and lists missing information with clarifying questions. The minimum-length fallbacks exist because the `AIGeneratedDetails` response model would otherwise return a 500 error. `_short_title` builds a title from the first clause when there is no AI.

sections.title: Duplicates, recommendations, correlation
sections.explanation: `find_duplicates` loads open and resolved incidents and runs the detector. `profiles` builds a `TechnicianProfile` for each active technician from incident history (open load, resolutions in the same category or service, average resolution time). `recommend` ranks them with `SmartRecommendationStrategy` from tour step 7. `suggest_resolutions` and `related_incidents` use plain token Jaccard. `correlation_clusters` groups recent open incidents by service and flags any group at or above the threshold as a likely shared root cause.

backend/app/domain/sla.py.overview: Pure SLA domain helpers with no I/O. The module builds an SLA record from a policy when an incident is created, defines the at-risk window as the last 25% of the resolution time, and evaluates an SLA dict as ON_TRACK, AT_RISK, BREACHED or MET at a given moment. The background SlaMonitor and the Incident model both depend on these functions (tour step 11).

sections.title: Time helpers
sections.explanation: `utcnow` always returns an aware UTC datetime. `parse_dt` accepts datetimes, ISO strings (including a trailing 'Z') or empty values, and makes the result timezone-aware. Mongo documents store timestamps as ISO strings, so this normalisation is what makes the comparisons later in the file safe. On bad input it returns `None` instead of raising.

sections.title: build_sla
sections.explanation: Copies the policy's response and resolution minutes into the incident, with defaults of 60 and 480, and computes absolute due timestamps from the creation time. Storing a snapshot means that later edits to a policy do not change deadlines already promised on existing incidents. New SLAs start as ON_TRACK.

sections.title: At-risk window
sections.explanation: `AT_RISK_FRACTION = 0.25` means the warning starts when a quarter of the resolution window remains. The window scales with priority: the docstring's examples are 7.5 minutes for a 30-minute P1 and 6 hours for a 24-hour P4. Keeping it proportional avoids early alarms on long SLAs and very late ones on short SLAs.

sections.title: evaluate_sla
sections.explanation: Returns a new dict (it never mutates the input) with two breach flags and a status. A deadline counts as breached if it was met late, or if it is still unmet and has passed. Resolved incidents become MET only if neither deadline was breached. Open incidents are BREACHED, then AT_RISK inside the window, otherwise ON_TRACK. The optional `now` parameter makes the function easy to test deterministically.

backend/app/services/sla_monitor.py.overview: The background SLA loop that server.py starts at startup (tour step 2). The docstring says it runs every 60 seconds. On each pass it re-evaluates every open incident's SLA, publishes at-risk events, records breaches, and escalates unacknowledged high-priority incidents through three levels, from Team Lead to IT Manager. It reports changes as events on the EventBus (tour step 8), so notifications and the audit trail are handled by observers. This file is the operational half of tour step 11.

sections.title: Escalation matrix docstring
sections.explanation: The docstring is the specification. Level 1 is triggered at 50% of the response window, level 2 at 100% (response SLA missed, with auto-dispatch), and level 3 at 200%. Each level has its own audience. The imports show the dependencies: domain enums, events, the Incident aggregate, the SYSTEM actor and the SLA time helpers.

sections.title: EscalationLevel and EscalationPolicy
sections.explanation: `EscalationLevel` is an immutable value object, and `LEVELS` is the ordered escalation ladder. `due_level` applies only to configured priorities, only while the incident is unacknowledged, and only in the NEW, CLASSIFIED or ASSIGNED states. It returns the highest level that is due and above the current one, so a monitor that was offline for a while jumps straight to the right level instead of sending several escalations at once.

sections.title: SlaMonitor wiring and recipients
sections.explanation: The monitor receives its repositories, the event bus and the IncidentService through its constructor, so it can be tested with fakes. `_publish` wraps the IncidentEvent boilerplate and attributes the event to the SYSTEM actor. `_recipients` chooses technicians skilled in the incident's category for 'team' levels, falling back to all technicians if none match, and administrators otherwise.

sections.title: run_once: the monitoring pass
sections.explanation: For each open incident with an SLA, `refresh_sla` returns the old and new status. An AT_RISK event is published only on the transition into that status, which prevents repeated warnings. Escalation can be switched off in settings. Note that the policy priorities come from `settings.get('escalation_priorities') or []`, so with no setting the empty list means no incident escalates. Changes are saved only when `incident.changes()` reports any, and breaches are recorded through the service. At level 2 or above, an unassigned CLASSIFIED incident is auto-assigned. An assignment failure is logged rather than raised, so one bad incident cannot stop the loop.

frontend/src/App.js.overview: The React application's main module, at nearly 2,000 lines. It holds the `useAuth` session hook, the top-level router, the login screen (password, 2FA, password reset and Google sign-in), the role-aware `Shell` with sidebar navigation and nested routes, and several pages defined inline: the incident list, the AI-assisted NewIncident form, user administration, notifications and docs. Tour step 12 covers the auth, routing and shell parts. The NewIncident form is where the frontend uses the intelligence endpoints from tour step 10.

sections.title: Imports and helpers
sections.explanation: Pulls in React Router, lucide icons, the `sonner` toasts, the shared axios client and the ErrorBoundary, plus page components from `./pages` and campus data from `./components`. `BITS_DOMAIN` restricts self-registration to campus email addresses. `extractStudentId` takes a 6 to 10 digit ID from the email prefix, or strips leading letters as a fallback. It is used both for the live ID preview on login and to prefill the report form.

sections.title: useAuth session hook
sections.explanation: Keeps the current user in state, initialised from localStorage, and re-fetches `/auth/me` on mount so role or activation changes made by an admin take effect on reload. `saveSession` is the only place that writes both the token and the user. `login` returns `{ mfaRequired, mfaToken }` instead of a user when the account uses an authenticator app, and `verifyTwoFactor` completes that second step. `logout` makes a best-effort call to the server, then always clears local state.

sections.title: App and top-level routes
sections.explanation: The root component creates `auth` once and passes it down as a prop instead of using a context. There are two routes: `/login` always shows the login screen, and every other path shows `Shell` if signed in or `Login` otherwise. This acts as a simple global auth guard.

sections.title: Login state and handlers
sections.explanation: One `mode` state switches between login, register, mfa, reset-request and reset-confirm, so a single component handles all sign-in flows. Every handler follows the same pattern: set busy, call the auth method, toast the result, navigate by role, clear busy. A 401 during 2FA sends the user back to the login step because the mfa token has expired. Google sign-in uses a full-page redirect. A `useRef` guard makes sure the reply in the URL fragment is consumed only once, and a `pageshow` listener re-enables the button when mobile browsers restore the page from cache.

sections.title: Shell layout and nested routes
sections.explanation: Works out the role flags, polls `/notifications` every 30 seconds and on every navigation for the bell count, and stores the dark-mode preference in localStorage. The sidebar links are filtered by role. A banner reminds administrators to set up 2FA. The nested `Routes` are wrapped in an `ErrorBoundary` keyed on the pathname, so a crash in one page leaves the sidebar usable and is cleared by navigating away. `AdminOnly` redirects non-admins in the client. The backend enforces the real authorisation.

sections.title: Incidents list
sections.explanation: Loads `/incidents` whenever the filters change. Search text is debounced by 250 ms, and a `cancelled` flag ignores responses from requests that have been superseded. Empty and false filters are dropped from the query. Technicians get an extra `scope` toggle (all, assigned or unassigned). Students see shortcut cards that link to `/incidents/new?type=...` presets. Each row shows location, priority, status, SLA badge and escalation level.

sections.title: NewIncident: state and live checks
sections.explanation: The form state `f` covers location mode (hostel, academics or online), category, service, impact and urgency, and the confirmation flags. The catalogue loads once and defaults to a carpentry repair. Two debounced effects run while the student types. The first calls `/intelligence/suggest` (350 ms) and auto-picks a category and service unless the student has already chosen one, which is tracked in the `touched` ref. The second calls `/intelligence/scope` with `use_ai: false` (400 ms) to show an emergency banner immediately.

sections.title: AI generation and submission
sections.explanation: `applyGenerated` maps the server's generated details onto the form, choosing a consistent location mode, category and service, then marks those fields as touched so later typing does not override them. `generateDetails` stops and shows the non-IT notice when the scope is out of bounds instead of filling in a ticket. `sendReport` checks scope again before submitting, using a per-text cache, and resolves the service actually submitted with `effectiveServiceId`. It then handles two server replies: an `OutOfScopeError` reopens the notice, and a 409 duplicate shows a warning with an acknowledgement checkbox.

sections.title: NewIncident form markup
sections.explanation: Renders the 'Generate Details with AI' button, the `NonItNotice` modal and the live `EmergencyBanner`, an AI triage summary card, the duplicate warning, and the form itself. The form includes one-click issue types from `ISSUE_TYPES`, the offline or online assistance choice, location pickers, contact details and the duplicate acknowledgement checkbox. Most logic lives in the handlers above, so this section is mainly declarative JSX.

sections.title: Users, notifications and docs pages
sections.explanation: `UsersPage` is the admin console. It lists accounts with role filters, creates admin and technician accounts (technicians with skills), toggles activation and resets a user's 2FA, all through `/admin/users`. `Notifications` loads the inbox, marks items read, and passes the unread count back to the Shell bell through `onChange`. `DOC_SECTIONS` and `Docs` render a static guide that summarises the lifecycle, roles, priority, assignment strategies, SLA escalation and intelligent features.

frontend/src/api.js.overview: The single axios client used by every page. It chooses the backend base URL, adds the JWT to every request, logs failed calls with the backend request ID, signs the user out on an expired token, and exports `errMsg` to turn FastAPI error payloads into readable text. It is the frontend half of the request path in tour step 12.

sections.title: Backend base URL resolution
sections.explanation: Uses `REACT_APP_BACKEND_URL` directly, except when it points at localhost and the page was opened from another device such as a phone on the same Wi-Fi or a tunnel. In that case 'localhost' would mean the phone itself, so the base becomes relative and the dev server forwards `/api` through setupProxy.js. `API` is exported so non-axios code such as errorReporting.js can use the same base URL.

sections.title: Client and auth interceptor
sections.explanation: A request interceptor reads `itsm_token` from localStorage on every call and sets the `Authorization: Bearer` header. Reading the token per request means a login or logout takes effect immediately, with no need to rebuild the client.

sections.title: Failure logging and 401 handling
sections.explanation: `logApiFailure` writes a collapsed console group with the method, URL, status, message and request ID, and points developers to the matching entry in `backend/logs/errors.log`. The response interceptor then handles expired or revoked tokens: on a 401 from anything other than a sign-in endpoint, it clears the session and does a hard redirect to `/login` instead of leaving the app half signed in. The error is still rejected, so callers can show their own toast.

sections.title: errMsg
sections.explanation: FastAPI returns `detail` as a string for business errors but as a list of objects for 422 validation errors. Rendering a list in a toast would crash React. `errMsg` handles network failures, string details (adding the request ID as a reference on 5xx), and validation lists (joining 'field: message' pairs with the `body` prefix removed).

frontend/src/errorReporting.js.overview: Browser-side error reporting. It sends uncaught errors, unhandled promise rejections and React render crashes to the backend's `POST /api/client-errors` endpoint, so they appear in the server's error log. It also provides an ErrorBoundary that shows a friendly recovery screen with a reference code instead of a blank page. index.js and App.js use the boundary at two levels (tour step 12).

sections.title: Rate limiting state
sections.explanation: Caps reports at 20 per page load and keeps a `recent` map of message to timestamp, so a render loop cannot flood the backend. `makeReference` creates a short `ui-xxxxxx` code that users can quote to an administrator. `clip` truncates fields to bounded sizes before they are sent.

sections.title: reportClientError
sections.explanation: Drops a report if the per-page cap is reached or the same message was sent in the last 30 seconds. It uses `fetch` with `keepalive: true`, so the request can finish even if the page is being unloaded, and attaches the token when one exists. The whole function is wrapped in try/catch and the fetch promise's rejection is swallowed, because, as the comment says, error reporting must never cause another error.

sections.title: Global error handlers
sections.explanation: Subscribes to `window` 'error' and 'unhandledrejection' events. Known noise is ignored: ResizeObserver loop warnings and opaque cross-origin 'Script error' messages. For rejected axios calls, the backend `request_id` is passed along, so the client and server log entries can be linked.

sections.title: ErrorBoundary component
sections.explanation: A class component, because React only supports error boundaries through `getDerivedStateFromError` and `componentDidCatch`. The first assigns a reference code, and the second logs to the console and reports the crash with the component stack. `componentDidUpdate` clears the error when `resetKey` changes, which is how Shell's pathname key resets it on navigation. The fallback UI offers Try again, Reload and Go to my reports, and the `fullPage` prop centres it for the outermost boundary.

frontend/src/index.js.overview: The browser entry point. It installs the global error handlers before anything renders, then mounts `App` inside a full-page ErrorBoundary with React 18's `createRoot`. This is the first frontend file in tour step 12.

sections.title: Imports
sections.explanation: Imports React, the React 18 `createRoot` API, global CSS, the App component, and the error-reporting utilities.

sections.title: Bootstrap
sections.explanation: `installGlobalErrorHandlers()` runs first, so errors raised while the app initialises are still reported. The outer `ErrorBoundary fullPage` is the last line of defence. App.js adds an inner, per-route boundary, so most crashes are caught there and the sidebar stays visible.

frontend/src/setupProxy.js.overview: Development-only proxy configuration that Create React App's dev server loads automatically. It forwards `/api` requests to the FastAPI backend, so the app works when opened from another device or through a tunnel. It pairs with the base-URL logic in api.js (tour step 12).

sections.title: Dev-server /api proxy
sections.explanation: Uses `http-proxy-middleware`, which ships with react-scripts, to forward `/api` to `BACKEND_PROXY_TARGET` (default `http://localhost:8000`). `changeOrigin` rewrites the Host header for the backend. Because requests are same-origin from the browser's point of view, no CORS changes are needed and the backend port is not exposed. api.js switches to relative URLs in exactly the case where this proxy is needed.

frontend/src/components/common.js.overview: Small shared presentation helpers used across the role-based pages (tour step 13): date and duration formatting, role and status labels, the Badge, Loading, Empty and Modal components, and the canonical lists of priorities, statuses and SLA statuses used by filters and badges.

sections.title: Formatting helpers
sections.explanation: `fmt` and `fmtShort` format timestamps in the user's locale. `roleLabel` maps internal role names to display text; in particular, the `customer` role is shown as STUDENT. `statusLabel` turns `IN_PROGRESS` into 'In progress'. `minutesLabel` picks minutes, hours or days, and `timeLeft` describes an SLA deadline as 'left' or 'overdue', which the incident pages use to show countdowns.

sections.title: Shared UI components
sections.explanation: `Badge` turns any value into a CSS class (`P1`, `AT_RISK` becomes `at-risk`), so priority, status and SLA badges are all styled from the stylesheet. `Modal` closes on Escape through a keydown listener that is cleaned up on unmount, and closes on backdrop click. `stopPropagation` on the content keeps clicks inside the dialog from closing it. The `wide` prop widens the dialog for larger forms.

sections.title: Enumeration constants
sections.explanation: The frontend copies of the backend's priority, incident status and SLA status values. They must stay in sync with the backend enums (tour step 6). `STATUSES` lists the lifecycle in order, from NEW to CLOSED.

frontend/src/pages/AdminConfig.js.overview: Administrator configuration screen, split into four tabs: strategies and automation, IT services, categories and SLA policies. It is the UI counterpart of the backend admin router from tour Step 7, letting an admin pick the assignment and priority strategies by name, tune escalation and correlation, and maintain the catalogue and SLA policies that the IncidentService relies on. Each tab is a self-contained function component that loads its own data through the shared axios client and reports outcomes with toast messages.

sections.title: Imports and tab definitions
sections.explanation: Imports React hooks, the `sonner` toast helper, lucide icons, the shared `api` client with its `errMsg` helper, and shared UI pieces (`Loading`, `Empty`, `Modal`, `minutesLabel`, `PRIORITIES`) from `components/common`. `TABS` is an array of `[key, label]` pairs, so the tab bar and the conditional rendering below are both driven from one list.

sections.title: Tabbed page shell
sections.explanation: `AdminConfig` keeps the selected tab in state, initialised lazily from `localStorage` so an admin returns to the tab they last used. Both the read and the write are wrapped in `try/catch` because `localStorage` can throw (for example in private browsing), and the page should still work then. The tab buttons carry `role="tab"` and `aria-selected` for accessibility, and exactly one child panel is rendered with short-circuit `&&` checks.

sections.title: Strategy settings state and save
sections.explanation: `StrategySettings` fetches `/admin/settings` once and keeps two copies: `data` (the server reply, including the lists of available strategies) and `form` (the editable settings). The `set` helper uses a functional state update so rapid changes never overwrite each other, and `togglePriority` adds or removes a priority from `escalation_priorities` while keeping the list sorted. `save` PUTs the whole form and replaces both copies with the server's answer, so whatever validation the backend applied is reflected immediately.

sections.title: Assignment and priority pickers
sections.explanation: The two radio lists are rendered from `data.assignment_strategies` and `data.priority_strategies`, which come from the backend factories rather than being hard-coded. That is the Strategy pattern from Step 7 surfacing in the UI: adding a new strategy class to the backend registry makes it appear here with its name and description, with no frontend change. A checkbox toggles `auto_assign_on_create`, which makes the service run the selected assignment strategy as soon as an incident is reported.

sections.title: Escalation, correlation and 2FA
sections.explanation: These panels edit the automation settings consumed by the SLA monitor and correlation detection: whether escalation is enabled and for which priorities, and how many reports within how many minutes count as a possible major incident. The ordered list documents the three escalation levels (Team Lead at 50% of response time, System Administrator on breach with auto-dispatch, IT Manager at 200%) so admins understand what they are switching on. A final panel toggles `require_admin_2fa`, and a sticky Save button disables itself while a save is in flight.

sections.title: IT services list
sections.explanation: `CRIT` maps the 1-3 criticality scale to labels; the panel text notes that criticality feeds the priority calculation. `Services` loads rows through a memoised `load` callback (via `useCallback`) so it can be reused after every save or delete. `save` chooses PUT or POST depending on whether the form has an `id`, and the delete button is disabled when `incident_count > 0`, mirroring the backend rule that in-use services cannot be removed (it returns 409).

sections.title: Service form
sections.explanation: `ServiceForm` copies the initial values into local state so edits stay private until the user submits. On submit it prevents the default page reload and trims the name before handing it to `onSave`. HTML validation attributes (`required`, `minLength`, `maxLength`) give quick feedback in the browser, while the backend still performs the real validation.

sections.title: Categories tab
sections.explanation: `Categories` uses a small inline form to add a category by name and shows every category as a chip with its incident count. As with services, the delete button is disabled when the category is in use, and a `window.confirm` dialog guards deletion. After any change it calls `load()` again instead of patching local state, keeping the UI consistent with the server at the cost of one extra request.

sections.title: SLA policies list and save
sections.explanation: `SlaPolicies` loads policies plus the service catalogue (for the service dropdown). `save` builds a clean request body, converting the minute fields to numbers with unary `+` and turning an empty service into `null`. The rows are sorted by priority and then put default (service-less) policies before service-specific ones. Default policies cannot be deleted, so their delete button is disabled with an explanatory tooltip; the feature tests check the matching 409 response on the backend.

sections.title: SLA policy editor modal
sections.explanation: The modal edits whichever policy is in `editing`. For an existing default policy (`id` set but no `service_id`) the priority and service dropdowns are disabled, so only the timings of defaults can change. New policies must pick a service, enforced by a disabled placeholder option and by disabling the Save button until a service is chosen. The resolution input's `min` follows the response time, a client-side hint for the backend rule that resolution cannot be shorter than response.

frontend/src/pages/Dashboard.js.overview: Operational dashboard for technicians and admins. It reads a single aggregate payload from the backend's `/reports/overview` endpoint and turns it into metric tiles, a possible-major-incident callout, severity, service and category bar charts, a technician workload table and recent SLA violations. It refreshes itself every 30 seconds and links into the incident queue and individual incidents, making it the at-a-glance view of the SLA and correlation features described in tour Step 13.

sections.title: Imports
sections.explanation: Pulls in React hooks, `Link` for in-app navigation, a set of lucide icons for the metric tiles, the shared `api` client and `errMsg`, and the shared `Badge`, `Loading`, `minutesLabel` and `fmtShort` helpers from `components/common`.

sections.title: Polling data load
sections.explanation: The effect defines `load`, calls it once, then repeats it every 30 seconds with `setInterval`; the cleanup function clears the timer when the page unmounts, which avoids leaks and state updates on an unmounted component. Errors are turned into a readable message with `errMsg`. Before rendering, the component computes maximum values for each chart (with `Math.max(1, ...)` so an empty dataset never divides by zero) to scale the bar widths.

sections.title: Metric tiles
sections.explanation: Two rows of `Metric` tiles show totals (all, open, P1 open, resolved) and SLA health (open breaches, compliance rate, escalated incidents, average resolution time). Each tile can carry a `sub` line with secondary detail such as how many incidents are at risk or how many were resolved today. All values come straight from `d.totals` and `d.sla`, so the backend owns the arithmetic.

sections.title: Possible major incidents
sections.explanation: When the backend reports correlations (several open reports on one service), a callout lists each service with its count, a suggestion and up to five incident links. Optional chaining (`d.correlations?.length`) keeps the page safe if the field is missing. This is where the correlation detection from the IncidentService becomes visible to staff.

sections.title: Severity breakdown
sections.explanation: Renders one item per priority with a horizontal track whose width is the count relative to the busiest priority. The CSS class is derived from the priority name (`severity-p1` and so on) so styling, not logic, decides the colours. A small detail: the label switches between 'incident' and 'incidents' based on the count.

sections.title: Service and category bars
sections.explanation: Two side-by-side panels draw simple CSS bar charts using inline `width` percentages rather than a charting library. The service list also shows how many incidents are open and, when present, how many breached their SLA. The category panel uses the same `bar-row` structure with an empty `<small />` so both lists line up in the grid.

sections.title: Workload and SLA violations
sections.explanation: The workload table lists active technicians with an open/capacity bar capped at 100% and marked `full` when they reach `max_concurrent`; the signed-in user's row is highlighted with '(you)'. The violations panel lists recent missed response or resolution deadlines with links to the incident and a priority badge. Finally it shows which assignment and priority strategies are active and, only for admins, a link to change them in AdminConfig.

sections.title: Metric tile component
sections.explanation: `Metric` is a tiny presentational component: an icon, a label, a large value and an optional secondary line. Keeping it local to this file (not exported) signals that it is only used by the dashboard.

frontend/src/pages/IncidentDetail.js.overview: The single-incident page and the richest screen in the frontend. It loads `/incidents/:id`, which returns the incident together with the role-specific `allowed_transitions`, the audit trail, related incidents, suggested resolutions and technician recommendations, and renders them as panels. Action buttons are generated from `allowed_transitions`, so the State pattern on the backend (tour Step 6) decides what each role may do; this page only labels the moves and collects extra data for resolve, close and edit.

sections.title: Imports
sections.explanation: Imports React hooks, router helpers (`Link`, `useParams`), toast notifications, many lucide icons, the shared API client, shared formatting and badge helpers from `components/common`, and the campus lists `ACADEMIC_BLOCKS` and `HOSTELS` used by the edit form's location pickers.

sections.title: Action labels and audit icons
sections.explanation: `actionLabel` turns a raw transition into friendly button text. The `IN_PROGRESS` target is special-cased because it means different things depending on where the incident comes from: reopening after RESOLVED, resuming after PENDING_INFO (with customer-specific wording) or starting work. Other targets use a lookup table with a generic fallback. `AUDIT_ICON` maps each audit action name to an emoji for the history timeline.

sections.title: State, loading and role flags
sections.explanation: The component keeps the loaded payload, an error message, the note being typed, which modal is open and the form state for resolving and closing. `load` is memoised on `id` and used both as the effect and as the refresh after every action. Once data is available it derives role flags (`isTech`, `isAdmin`, `isStaff`) and `canSelfAssign`, which is true only for a technician looking at an unassigned incident in CLASSIFIED or ASSIGNED.

sections.title: Action helpers
sections.explanation: `run` is a small wrapper used by every action: it sets `busy`, awaits the request, shows a success toast, closes any modal and reloads, or shows the error message on failure. `transition` posts to `/incidents/:id/transition`, and `onAction` intercepts RESOLVED and CLOSED to open a modal first, since those moves need a resolution summary or feedback. Notes are posted with a `kind` that depends on whether the author is staff or the reporter.

sections.title: Header and action bar
sections.explanation: The header shows the incident number, status and priority badges, a location pill, an escalation badge when the SLA monitor has escalated it, and the SLA status with time remaining. A warning callout tells a customer what to do when the incident is waiting on them (PENDING_INFO). The action bar combines self-assign for technicians, auto-dispatch for admins, one button per entry in `d.allowed_transitions`, and an Edit button for staff while the incident is open.

sections.title: Details, SLA and outcome panels
sections.explanation: Two key-value panels show reporter contact details and the classification/assignment data, including the priority score and the strategy that produced it. The SLA panel renders two `SlaBox` components (response and resolution) and, if present, the escalation history as badges. Resolution and closure cards appear only once those stages have happened, including the star rating left by the reporter.

sections.title: Staff-only intelligence panels
sections.explanation: Three panels are shown only to staff: suggested resolutions from similar past incidents (with a 'Use this fix' button that prefills the resolve form when RESOLVED is an allowed move), possible duplicates and related incidents (filtered so an incident is not listed twice), and smart technician recommendations with match scores. Admins can assign any recommended technician, while a technician can only pick up the incident for themselves. The backend also hides suggested resolutions from customers, so this page and the API agree.

sections.title: Notes and history timeline
sections.explanation: The notes panel lists existing notes and, unless the incident is closed, a textarea whose placeholder changes with the user's role. The history panel renders the audit trail written by the audit observer (Step 8) as a timeline, showing actor, role and the previous-to-new state when a status change occurred. Closed incidents hide the note input because the backend treats them as read-only and would reject the request with 409.

sections.title: Resolve, close and edit modals
sections.explanation: The resolve modal requires a summary and optionally a root cause, then calls `transition('RESOLVED', ...)` with those fields. The close modal collects a 1-5 star rating through accessible radio-style buttons and an optional comment; an empty comment is sent as `undefined` so it is omitted from the JSON. The edit modal delegates to `EditIncident` and saves through a PATCH request.

sections.title: SlaBox and EditIncident
sections.explanation: `SlaBox` derives a visual state (`ok`, `late` or `pending`) from whether the target was met and whether it was breached, and flags breaches as recorded SLA violations. `EditIncident` seeds a form from the incident and its nested location, then on submit sends only fields that actually changed (treating an empty string and a missing value as equal), and simply closes when nothing changed. The note at the bottom reminds staff that changing impact, urgency, criticality or affected people makes the backend recalculate priority and SLA.

backend/tests/conftest.py.overview: pytest's shared configuration for the backend test suite. It contains no fixtures; instead it sets environment variables at import time so that the application, when imported by the test modules, connects to a throwaway database and never reaches real external services. This is the isolation layer described in tour Step 14.

sections.title: Imports
sections.explanation: Only `os` and `tempfile` are needed: the file works purely by editing the process environment before the app is imported.

sections.title: Test environment overrides
sections.explanation: Because pytest loads `conftest.py` before the test modules, these assignments run before `server` and `app.core.db` read their settings. The comment explains the key trick: `load_dotenv()` does not override variables that are already set, so these values win over `backend/.env`. `DB_NAME` and `JWT_SECRET` use `setdefault` (a caller can still override them), while SMTP and all Gemini key variables are forcibly blanked so tests never send email or call the real API. Logs go to a fresh temporary directory.

backend/tests/test_domain.py.overview: Fast unit tests for the pure domain layer: priority strategies, assignment strategies with capacity rules, and the State pattern's role-checked transitions. They need no database or HTTP client, constructing domain objects directly. The tests are written in a very compact style, often one assertion per line, and complement the end-to-end tests in test_features.py.

sections.title: Wildcard imports
sections.explanation: Star imports bring in the strategies, enums, `StateFactory` and exception classes. This keeps the tests short, though it hides where each name comes from; the names used (for example `PriorityInput`, `TechnicianProfile`, `InvalidStateTransitionError`) are defined in the domain modules covered in tour Steps 6 and 7.

sections.title: Core smoke tests
sections.explanation: Four compact tests: the weighted-score strategy maps maximum inputs to P1 and minimum inputs to P4; `PriorityInput` rejects an impact of 0 with `InvalidInputError`; NEW cannot jump straight to CLOSED even for an admin; and the skill-based strategy picks a technician whose skills match the incident category. `pytest` is imported inside each function that needs `pytest.raises`.

sections.title: Matrix priority and capacity
sections.explanation: The matrix priority tests check the impact/urgency grid at its corners and edges (P1 through P4). The capacity tests show that `LoadBalancedStrategy` refuses a technician who is at `max_concurrent` for a P3 incident by raising `TechnicianUnavailableError`, but allows the same technician for a P1, encoding the rule that critical incidents may exceed capacity. The smart strategy test checks that its ranking exposes a score breakdown with exactly five factors.

sections.title: State transition rules
sections.explanation: These tests exercise the State pattern directly through `StateFactory.get(...)`: CLOSED is terminal, a customer can verify a RESOLVED incident while a technician cannot (raising `UnauthorizedOperationError`), and a customer can move a PENDING_INFO incident back to IN_PROGRESS after supplying information. They pin down the role-dependent rules that IncidentDetail.js later presents as buttons.

backend/tests/test_features.py.overview: End-to-end feature tests for the project brief. A few tests unit-check the OOP domain model, but most drive the real FastAPI app in-process through an httpx `ASGITransport` client, logging in as the seeded demo users and checking API responses, notifications, the audit trail and SLA violations in the test database. Together they verify the patterns from the tour (factories, State, Strategy, Observer-driven audit and notifications, SLA escalation, correlation) working together.

sections.title: Docstring and imports
sections.explanation: The docstring lists what is covered. The imports bring in the ASGI app, the composition-root `container` (so tests can inspect repositories and call the SLA monitor directly), `init_db`, enums, exceptions, domain classes and strategies. Importing `IncidentStatus as S` keeps status comparisons short.

sections.title: Fixtures and request helpers
sections.explanation: `anyio_backend` pins async tests to asyncio, and the module-scoped autouse `setup_db` fixture initialises the database (indexes and seed data) once, then restores default settings afterwards so tests that change strategies do not leak. `client()` builds an `AsyncClient` bound to the app with no network involved. Helpers `login`, `service_id`, `report` and `notifications_for` hide the boilerplate; `report` uses `time.time_ns()` in titles and sets `acknowledge_duplicate` so repeated runs are not blocked by duplicate detection.

sections.title: Domain model unit tests
sections.explanation: These synchronous tests check that `UserFactory` builds the right subclass and validates input, that `can_view` is polymorphic per user type, and that technician capacity is enforced at exactly the limit with a P1 override. They also confirm that a new incident starts in NEW and that the lifecycle rejects illegal or unauthorised moves, that service criticality raises the weighted priority, and that every registered assignment strategy can be swapped in through the factory and still returns a valid technician.

sections.title: Creation audit and strategy switching
sections.explanation: The first API test reports a high-impact incident on a critical service and checks the result is P1 and CLASSIFIED, that the audit trail records creation, classification, priority calculation and SLA application, and that admins receive a `critical` notification. The second test shows that an unknown strategy name is rejected with 422, that switching to `load` makes auto-assign choose the least-loaded technician, and that the audit entry mentions the strategy used, before switching back to `smart`.

sections.title: Notification lifecycle
sections.explanation: Walks an incident through assignment, acknowledgement, pending info, a customer note, resumption, resolution with a root cause, verification and closure. After each step it checks that the right person received the right notification kind (for example `assignment` for the technician, `info_requested` and `resolved` for the customer). It also checks that a feedback rating of 6 is rejected with 422 and that adding a note to a closed incident returns 409.

sections.title: SLA monitor and escalation
sections.explanation: Instead of waiting in real time, these tests call `container.sla_monitor.run_once(now=...)` with simulated timestamps after creation. They check the escalation ladder (level 1 Team Lead at more than 50% of the response window, level 2 with auto-dispatch once the SLA is breached, level 3 at 200%), that repeated runs do not duplicate violations, and that both response and resolution violations end up in the audit trail and admin listing. A second test checks that an at-risk P4 incident warns its assigned technician.

sections.title: Correlation and suggested fixes
sections.explanation: The correlation test creates a fresh service, reports four incidents on it and expects exactly one admin alert, a correlation cluster with count 4, related incidents on the detail page and an entry in the overview report. The suggested-resolution test resolves an Outlook crash, reports a similar one, and expects the first as the top suggestion for staff, while the customer sees an empty list.

sections.title: Search filters and admin catalogue
sections.explanation: The search test loops over a dictionary of filters (text, status, priority, category, service, SLA status, date range, unassigned) and checks the new incident is found by each one, plus 422 for an unparseable date. The admin test checks that students get 403, that duplicate names return 409, that a service-specific SLA policy overrides the default and is used for a new incident, and that in-use services, categories and default SLA policies cannot be deleted.

sections.title: Error paths and admin edits
sections.explanation: Covers failure handling: deleting the default P4 policy (restored in a `finally` block) makes incident creation fail with a 500 and a `MissingSlaConfigError` body; admins can edit technician skills (deduplicated) and capacity, and filter the audit log by action or incident; wrong passwords return 401 with `AuthenticationError`; a set of invalid report payloads return 404 or 422; and students cannot edit or auto-assign incidents (403).

backend/tests/test_gemini.py.overview: Edge-case tests for the Gemini adapter in the intelligence service (tour Step 10). Most tests replace Google's API with `httpx.MockTransport`, so they run offline and can simulate malformed, hostile or failing replies; they check that the adapter either returns cleaned, range-limited data or returns `None` so the keyword classifier takes over. A middle group drives the API endpoints with a swapped-in fake adapter, and a final group of `live` tests calls the real API only when a key is configured and Google is reachable.

sections.title: Setup and mock helpers
sections.explanation: The docstring explains the offline/live split. `GOOD` is a valid model reply used as a baseline that tests modify with `{**GOOD, ...}`. `gemini_reply` wraps text in Gemini's response envelope, `adapter` builds a `GeminiAdapter` with a mock transport and no retry delay, and `answering` returns a handler that records every request in `handler.calls` and can simulate a JSON reply, an HTTP error status or a raised network exception. `classify` is a shortcut for the common call.

sections.title: Well-formed and slightly-off replies
sections.explanation: Checks that a valid reply is used and that the API key is sent only in the `x-goog-api-key` header, never in the URL, and that the user text is wrapped in `<report>` tags in the prompt. Other tests show the adapter's tolerance: JSON wrapped in markdown fences or prose is extracted, numbers given as words or strings are parsed, out-of-range values are clamped, categories are matched case-insensitively (unknown ones become `None`), missing or wrongly typed fields get safe defaults, and long or multi-line text is trimmed.

sections.title: Unusable replies and failures
sections.explanation: Each case here must return `None` so the caller falls back to keyword rules: truncated JSON, plain prose, JSON that is not an object, empty text, a safety-blocked prompt (which must also be logged), and HTTP bodies that are not the expected shape. The parametrised HTTP-error test checks that client errors (400-429) are not retried and that the log contains a helpful hint without leaking the key. Server errors (503) are retried exactly once, and timeouts or connection errors return `None`.

sections.title: Configuration and prompt safety
sections.explanation: `from_env` must return `None` when no usable key is set and must trim whitespace and default the model name. Model names that could alter the request URL (path traversal, query strings, spaces) are replaced by the default. The prompt is capped in length with control characters stripped, and a prompt-injection test shows that a hostile reply still produces only valid, clamped data while the prompt itself tells the model to ignore instructions inside the report.

sections.title: API fixture and adapter swap
sections.explanation: The `api` fixture initialises the database, opens an in-process client logged in as the demo customer, and after the test restores `container.intel.classifier_factory` to `GeminiAdapter.from_env`. `use_gemini` replaces that factory with one that builds a mock-backed adapter. This is the composition root from Step 3 paying off: the service's collaborator is swapped in one line without touching application code.

sections.title: Endpoint behaviour with Gemini
sections.explanation: Through the real `/api/intelligence` routes, these tests check that an unknown AI category falls back to the keyword category, that tiny AI-generated title or description fields are replaced with usable text, and that the endpoint still answers 200 (with the keyword classifier's lower confidence) when Gemini errors, is unreachable or returns garbage. Hindi, Telugu, emoji-heavy and maximum-length inputs must never break the endpoint, and descriptions that are empty, too short or too long are rejected with 422.

sections.title: Live API tests
sections.explanation: `_live_key` reads `LLM_API_KEY` from `backend/.env` with `dotenv_values` (not from the environment, which conftest.py blanked), and `_reachable` also pings Google; the `live` marker skips these tests when either check fails. When they do run, they check that a real reply is valid, that a prompt-injection attempt still yields an allowed category and impact, that non-English or gibberish input is handled, and that an invalid key results in a clean `None`.

backend/.env.example.overview: Template for the backend's environment configuration. start.sh copies it to `backend/.env` on the first run (replacing `JWT_SECRET` with a random value), and docker-compose.yml loads it as the base env file for the backend container. It documents every setting the backend reads: database, CORS, authentication, seeded admin, Google sign-in, SMTP, Gemini and logging.

sections.title: Database, CORS and secrets
sections.explanation: `MONGO_URL` and `DB_NAME` point at a local MongoDB; docker-compose overrides the URL to reach the `mongo` service. `CORS_ORIGINS` allows the React dev server. `JWT_SECRET` is a placeholder that must be replaced, which start.sh does automatically. The comment on `TOTP_ENCRYPTION_KEY` warns that changing it (or changing `JWT_SECRET` while it is unset) invalidates stored authenticator-app secrets.

sections.title: Admin and sign-in settings
sections.explanation: `ADMIN_EMAIL` and `ADMIN_PASSWORD` define the seeded admin account used throughout the tests. `GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID` and `ALLOWED_EMAIL_DOMAIN` configure Google sign-in restricted to the campus email domain, and `COOKIE_SECURE=false` suits local HTTP development.

sections.title: Email and AI
sections.explanation: SMTP host and port are prefilled for Gmail, but the credentials are blank so real email is off by default. `LLM_API_KEY` is also blank, which makes the app use its built-in keyword rules; `LLM_MODEL` selects the Gemini model the adapter will call.

sections.title: Logging
sections.explanation: Logging settings referenced from the README's error-log section: the log level, an optional log directory, the threshold in milliseconds above which a request counts as slow, and whether to write full tracebacks.

backend/Dockerfile.overview: Container image definition for the FastAPI backend, used by docker-compose.yml's `backend` service. It is a minimal six-line build on `python:3.12-slim` that installs the pinned requirements and runs the app with uvicorn on port 8000.

sections.title: Base image and dependencies
sections.explanation: Starts from the slim Python 3.12 image and sets `/app` as the working directory. `requirements.txt` is copied and installed on its own before the source code, so Docker can reuse the cached dependency layer when only code changes. `--no-cache-dir` keeps pip's download cache out of the image.

sections.title: Source and start command
sections.explanation: Copies the rest of the backend into the image and starts `uvicorn server:app` on `0.0.0.0:8000`, binding to all interfaces so the port is reachable from outside the container. docker-compose replaces this command with one that adds `--reload` for development.

docker-compose.yml.overview: Docker Compose definition that runs the whole stack with only Docker installed: MongoDB 7, the FastAPI backend on port 8000 and the React dev server on port 3000. It is set up for development, with source folders bind-mounted and auto-reload enabled, and data persisted in a named volume. It is the Docker alternative to start.sh covered in tour Step 15.

sections.title: Usage notes
sections.explanation: The header comments give the two commands needed (`docker compose up --build` and `docker compose down`) and explain that settings come from the `.env.example` files, overridden by real `.env` files when they exist.

sections.title: MongoDB service
sections.explanation: Runs the official `mongo:7` image with `restart: unless-stopped`. Its data directory is stored in the named volume `mongo_data`, so incidents and users survive `docker compose down`. No port is published, because only the backend container needs to reach it.

sections.title: Backend service
sections.explanation: Builds from `./backend` (the Dockerfile) and layers two env files: the required example file, then the optional real `.env`. `MONGO_URL` is overridden to `mongodb://mongo:27017` because services reach each other by service name on the Compose network. The command adds `--reload`, and the app package, `server.py` and logs are bind-mounted so code changes on the host take effect without rebuilding.

sections.title: Frontend service
sections.explanation: Builds the React app from `./frontend` with the same two-level env-file setup. `REACT_APP_BACKEND_URL` is empty so the browser calls `/api` on the same origin, and `BACKEND_PROXY_TARGET` tells the dev-server proxy (setupProxy.js) to forward those calls to `http://backend:8000`. `WATCHPACK_POLLING` makes file watching work through bind mounts, and `BROWSER: none` stops the dev server trying to open a browser inside the container.

sections.title: Named volume
sections.explanation: Declares the `mongo_data` volume used by the MongoDB service. Docker manages its storage, so it persists across container restarts and rebuilds until removed explicitly.

start.sh.overview: One-command setup and launch script for macOS and Linux. On the first run it creates the `.env` files, the Python virtual environment and `node_modules`; on every run it reinstalls only what changed, makes sure MongoDB is running, starts the backend and frontend, optionally opens a public ngrok tunnel and prints the links. Ctrl+C stops everything it started. It is the non-Docker path described in tour Step 15.

sections.title: Header and helpers
sections.explanation: The comments document usage (`--local` skips ngrok) and the optional `NGROK_URL` setting. The script moves to its own directory so it works from anywhere, creates `logs/`, and defines small helpers: `say` prints bold status lines, `fail` prints red and exits, and `env_value` reads one key from an env file, stripping quotes, spaces and carriage returns.

sections.title: Tool checks
sections.explanation: Tries several Python executables in order and keeps the first one that is at least 3.10, verified by actually running a version check. If no suitable Python or no `npm` is found, it stops with an install hint rather than failing later with a confusing error.

sections.title: Create settings files
sections.explanation: If `backend/.env` is missing, an inline Python heredoc copies `.env.example` and replaces the `JWT_SECRET` line with `secrets.token_urlsafe(48)`, so every installation gets its own random signing secret. `frontend/.env` is simply copied from its example. Existing files are never overwritten.

sections.title: Backend virtualenv
sections.explanation: If the venv's Python cannot run (missing, or copied from another machine), the venv is deleted and recreated. Packages are reinstalled only when `requirements.txt` differs from a stamp copy saved inside the venv (`cmp -s`), which makes repeat runs fast while still picking up dependency changes.

sections.title: Frontend packages
sections.explanation: Uses the same stamp-file technique: `npm install` runs only when `package.json` differs from the copy saved in `node_modules`. The install runs in a subshell so the `cd` does not affect the rest of the script.

sections.title: Ensure MongoDB is running
sections.explanation: `port_open` probes a TCP port using bash's `/dev/tcp` feature, with no extra tools. If `MONGO_URL` points at localhost and port 27017 is closed, the script tries Homebrew's `mongodb-community` service, otherwise starts or creates a `bits-mongo` Docker container, then waits up to 20 seconds. If MongoDB still is not reachable it exits with installation instructions.

sections.title: Cleanup trap and server start
sections.explanation: `stop_all` is registered on INT, TERM and EXIT; it removes the trap first to avoid running twice, then kills each background process and its children. `free_port` uses `lsof` to kill leftovers from an earlier run on ports 8000, 3000 and (when sharing) 4040. The backend (uvicorn with `--reload`) and frontend (`npm start`) are launched in background subshells using `exec`, and their PIDs are stored for cleanup.

sections.title: Optional ngrok tunnel
sections.explanation: `public_url` queries ngrok's local API and extracts the first HTTPS tunnel using a one-line Python JSON parser. `start_ngrok` launches ngrok for port 3000 (optionally with a fixed URL) and polls for up to 20 seconds, giving up early if the process dies. If a pinned URL fails, which happens when it belongs to another ngrok account, the script retries without it; on failure it shows the end of the ngrok log and an authtoken hint, and on success saves the URL to `logs/public-url.txt`.

sections.title: Ready banner and wait
sections.explanation: Because the React dev server clears the terminal when it finishes compiling, the script waits for port 3000 to answer (plus a few seconds) before printing the banner, so the links stay visible. The banner shows the local URL and, if available, the public URL along with the Google redirect URI that must be registered for sign-in to work there. `wait` keeps the script alive until the servers exit or the user presses Ctrl+C.

backend/app/routers/__init__.py.overview: Empty package marker for the FastAPI routers package; server.py imports the individual router modules from it.

backend/app/routers/client_errors.py.overview: FastAPI router that receives crash reports from the React frontend (render errors, uncaught errors, unhandled rejections), rate-limits them per IP and writes them to errors.log alongside backend errors.

backend/app/routers/docs.py.overview: Authenticated FastAPI endpoint returning in-app documentation about the incident lifecycle, the design patterns used and the intelligent features.

backend/tests/test_api_flow.py.overview: End-to-end API tests covering role logins, the full incident lifecycle, BITS student registration restrictions, admin user creation and campus location/intelligence handling against a clean test database.

backend/tests/test_autofill.py.overview: Tests keyword-based category and service autofill suggestions (IT vs hostel repair categories, whole-word matching, ranking) and the suggest API endpoint.

backend/tests/test_bug_fixes.py.overview: Regression tests for bugs fixed on 2026-11-01: password-reset enumeration, audit trail by incident number, reopen and SLA resume, resolution validation, technician isolation, priority recalculation, admin self-deactivation, reporting counts, classifier matching and Google account login.

backend/tests/test_duplicates_and_sla_de.overview: Tests concept-based duplicate detection across different wordings, the duplicate warning via the API, the default SLA targets from the project brief, upgrade of old seeded defaults, and P1 SLA at-risk evaluation.

backend/tests/test_error_logging.py.overview: Tests that unhandled errors return a reference and are logged fully, validation errors never leak passwords, business-rule errors explain why and where, browser errors are recorded, and MongoDB outages are explained.

backend/tests/test_form_autofill.py.overview: Tests that generate-details fills the whole report form (category, service, impact, urgency, criticality, location) with and without AI, plus campus location extraction and criticality estimation rules.

backend/tests/test_scope_api.py.overview: API tests for non-IT/emergency scope detection with and without AI: blocking non-IT submissions with guidance, reporter override, AI fallbacks and the safety-first rule that AI cannot override a detected crisis.

backend/tests/test_scope_rules.py.overview: Offline tests of the rule-based scope classifier using real-world phrasings that must stay IT tickets or must trigger emergency/non-IT guidance, plus AI answer parsing and safety-first combination.

frontend/src/components/EditUserModal.js.overview: Admin modal for editing a user's name and phone, plus skills and maximum concurrent incidents for technicians, saved via PATCH /admin/users/{id}.

frontend/src/components/IncidentFilters..overview: Search and filter bar for the incident list covering text, status, priority, category, service, technician, SLA status, date range and escalation, loading catalogue options from the backend.

frontend/src/components/NonItNotice.js.overview: Popup, contact list and inline banner shown when a report is detected as a non-IT emergency (medical, mental health, fire, security), directing the user to the right phone contacts.

frontend/src/components/campus.js.overview: Static campus reference data shared by the report form and incident editor: academic blocks, hostels, technician skills and offline repair categories mapped to support services.

frontend/src/components/issueTypes.js.overview: Catalogue of common campus issue templates (Wi-Fi, LAN, login, etc.) offered as one-click shortcuts on the report form, each mapped to mode, category, service, title and hint, with a lookup by key.

frontend/src/googleSignIn.js.overview: Google sign-in via full-page OpenID Connect implicit-flow redirect: builds the authorization URL with state/nonce, validates the secure-origin requirement, and parses the id_token returned in the URL hash.

frontend/src/pages/Account.js.overview: Self-service account page with panels for profile, password change, authenticator-app two-factor setup and backup codes, notification preferences, active sessions and recent security activity.

frontend/src/pages/AuditLog.js.overview: Admin page with a filterable audit trail of system actions and a list of recorded SLA violations.

backend/app/services/audit.py.overview: Backwards-compatibility shim re-exporting AuditRepository as AuditLogger; the audit trail now lives in the repositories module and is written by an observer.

backend/app/routers/account.py.overview: FastAPI router for the signed-in user's account and security page: profile edits, password change, authenticator-app (TOTP) setup/enable/disable, backup codes, email preferences, sign-out-everywhere, and recent security activity.

backend/app/routers/catalog.py.overview: Small read-only catalog router listing IT services, incident categories, and active technicians (staff-only) for form pickers and filters.

backend/app/routers/notifications.py.overview: In-app notifications router that lists a user's latest 50 notifications with an unread count and marks one or all notifications as read directly in MongoDB.

backend/app/routers/reports.py.overview: Reporting dashboard router whose single overview endpoint aggregates incident totals, status/priority/category/service breakdowns, SLA compliance, technician workload, recent SLA violations and correlation clusters for staff.

backend/app/services/__init__.py.overview: Empty package initializer marking backend/app/services as a Python package.

backend/app/services/two_factor.py.overview: TOTP two-factor authentication: Fernet-encrypted secrets, HMAC-hashed backup codes, QR provisioning, time-step matching, polymorphic TOTP/backup-code factors and a TwoFactorService with replay protection and brute-force lockout.

backend/tests/test_account_security.py.overview: Pytest suite for account security: TOTP encryption and code windows, email preferences, 2FA setup/sign-in/lockout/disable, authenticator password reset, password change, session sign-out, profile/preferences and admin 2FA controls via the HTTP API.

backend/.dockerignore.overview: Docker build-context exclusion list for the backend image, keeping the local virtualenv, Python bytecode, pytest cache, log files, the secret-bearing .env and macOS metadata out of the container.

frontend/.dockerignore.overview: Docker build-context exclusion list for the React frontend image, omitting node_modules, the production build output, the local .env and macOS metadata.

frontend/Dockerfile.overview: Single-stage node:20 image for the React frontend that installs npm dependencies from package*.json, copies the source and runs the development server via npm start.

start.bat.overview: Double-clickable Windows launcher that runs start.ps1 through PowerShell with the execution policy bypassed, forwarding arguments such as -Local and pausing on failure.

start.ps1.overview: Windows one-command setup and launch script: finds Python 3.10+ and Node, creates .env files with a generated JWT secret, (re)builds the backend venv and installs packages only when requirements change, starts MongoDB via service or Docker, launches backend and frontend in separate windows and optionally opens an ngrok public link.

backend/app/__init__.py.overview: Empty package marker that makes `app` an importable Python package; it contains no code or re-exports.

backend/app/core/__init__.py.overview: Empty package marker that makes `app/core` an importable Python package; it contains no code or re-exports.

backend/app/domain/__init__.py.overview: Empty package marker that makes `app/domain` an importable Python package; it contains no code or re-exports.

backend/app/models/__init__.py.overview: Empty package marker that makes `app/models` an importable Python package; it contains no code or re-exports.

frontend/.env.example.overview: Template of frontend build-time environment variables: REACT_APP_BACKEND_URL for the API base URL and REACT_APP_GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID for Google sign-in.

frontend/package.json.overview: Create React App manifest for the BITS reports frontend, defining start/build/test scripts via react-scripts and dependencies on React 18, react-router-dom, axios, recharts, lucide-react, sonner and Testing Library, plus browserslist targets.

frontend/public/index.html.overview: HTML shell for the React single-page app: sets the 'BITS reports | Campus IT Support' title, theme color and viewport, preloads Google Fonts (JetBrains Mono, Outfit, Plus Jakarta Sans, Syne), and provides the #root mount point with a noscript fallback.

frontend/src/index.css.overview: Global stylesheet for the entire frontend: CSS custom-property theme tokens and fonts, the fixed-sidebar app shell, login and account pages, dashboards, metrics, panels, modals, filters, incident timelines, SLA/severity badges and AI-assist UI, a warm palette override, a .dark-mode theme, and responsive breakpoints at 960px and 640px.
